file_too_large.why: A workflow file is read whole, so there is a limit on its size.
fix: Move long scripts out of the workflow, into files the steps run.
Split the workflow into smaller ones that call each other with uses:.

extra_document.why: A YAML file can hold several documents, separated by ---. A workflow is the first one; the rest is ignored.
fix: Remove the --- and what follows it, or move it into a workflow of its own.

extra_document_invalid.why: The file has a second YAML document after ---, which is ignored, and that document isn't valid YAML either.
fix: Remove the --- and what follows it.

yaml_syntax.why: The file isn't valid YAML, so it can't be read as a workflow.
fix: Check the line the error names, and the indentation of the lines before it.
Quote a value that holds a colon followed by a space, or starts with a character such as {, [, * or &.

yaml_alias.why: YAML aliases (*name) repeat a value marked with an anchor (&name). Workflows don't allow them, because a few aliases can make a small file expand to a huge one.
fix: Write the value out where the alias is.

yaml_collection_key.why: A workflow is JSON values, whose keys are strings. YAML allows a list or a mapping as a key, which JSON can't hold.
fix: Make the key a string.

yaml_merge_key.why: YAML merge keys (<<) copy one mapping into another. Workflows don't allow them, as they aren't part of YAML 1.2 and readers disagree on what they mean.
fix: Write out the keys the merge would copy.

duplicate_key.why: A key appears twice in the same mapping. Only its last value is used.
fix: Remove one of the two, or rename it if both were meant.

number_not_json.why: The value is a number YAML allows but JSON doesn't, such as .inf or .nan.
fix: Quote it if it is text, or write a finite number.

format_too_new.why: The workflow's format: names a format newer than the one this version of Meridian runs.
fix: Run the workflow with a newer version, or write it in an older format.

schema_failed.why: The workflow couldn't be checked against its format's schema. This is a problem in Meridian, not in the workflow.
fix: Report it, with the workflow that causes it.

unknown_key.why: The workflow has a key its format doesn't define here, so it is ignored. It is often a misspelling.
fix: Correct the key's spelling, or remove it.

unknown_key_unresolved.why: The workflow has a key its format doesn't define here, alongside other errors that make it unclear what was meant.
fix: Fix the other errors first, then correct or remove the key.

invalid_name.why: Names here, such as a job's or an input's, must match a pattern, so that expressions can read them.
fix: Rename it to use only the characters the pattern allows.

input_type_unknown.why: An input's type: isn't one of the types the format defines.
fix: Use one of the types the message lists.

workflow_empty.why: The file has no workflow in it.
fix: Add the workflow's jobs.

wrong_type.why: The value has a different type from the one the format expects here, such as a list where a string goes.
fix: Write the value as the type the message names.

missing_keys.why: A mapping is missing keys it must have.
fix: Add the keys the message lists.

missing_any_key.why: A mapping must have one of several keys, and has none of them.
fix: Add one of the keys the message lists.

not_expression.why: This value must be a ${{ }} expression, so that it is evaluated, not read as text.
fix: Write it as ${{ ... }}.

pattern_mismatch.why: The value doesn't have the form the format expects here.
fix: Write it in the form the message's pattern describes.

must_equal.why: Only one value is allowed here.
fix: Use the value the message names.

value_must_equal.why: Only one value is allowed here.
fix: Use the value the message names.

value_must_be_one_of.why: Only some values are allowed here.
fix: Use one of the values the message lists.

value_must_equal_or_expression.why: Only one value is allowed here, or a ${{ }} expression that gives it.
fix: Use the value the message names, or an expression.

value_must_be_one_of_or_expression.why: Only some values are allowed here, or a ${{ }} expression that gives one of them.
fix: Use one of the values the message lists, or an expression.

value_must_match.why: The value doesn't have any of the forms the format allows here.
fix: Write it in one of the forms the message's patterns describe.

too_few_keys.why: The mapping has fewer keys than the format requires here.
fix: Add keys until it has the minimum.

too_many_keys.why: The mapping has more keys than the format allows here.
fix: Remove keys until it is within the limit.

key_not_allowed.why: This key isn't allowed in this mapping, given the other keys it has.
fix: Remove the key, or the key it conflicts with.

keys_not_allowed_together.why: These keys each choose a different form for the mapping, so it can't have them together.
fix: Keep the keys of the form you mean, and remove the others.

form_not_allowed.why: The value has a form the format rules out here.
fix: Check the format's documentation for what is allowed here.

several_forms.why: The value matches more than one of the forms allowed here, so what it means isn't clear.
fix: Remove the keys that belong to the forms you don't mean.

no_form.why: The value matches none of the forms allowed here, and it isn't clear which one was meant.
fix: Check the format's documentation for the forms allowed here.

schema_rule.why: The value breaks one of the rules of the workflow's schema.
fix: Change the value as the message says.

input_not_json.why: A run's input values are JSON, and this one holds something JSON can't, such as NaN or text that isn't UTF-8. It was submitted that way, or an expression in the input's default gave it: 0/0 gives NaN, and 1/0 an infinity.
fix: Submit the value as JSON.
If the input's default gave it, change the expression so that it gives a value JSON can hold. A hyphen subtracts, so inputs.pw-user gives NaN: read the input as inputs['pw-user'].

unknown_input.why: A value was submitted for an input the workflow doesn't define. It is kept, since a workflow that another calls can read inputs it doesn't define, but it is often a misspelling.
fix: Correct the input's name, or remove the value.

input_group_not_mapping.why: A group of inputs takes a mapping of its inputs' values.
fix: Submit the group's value as a mapping, keyed by its inputs' names.

defaults_read_each_other.why: The defaults of these inputs read each other's values, so none of them can be worked out first.
fix: Change one of the defaults so that it doesn't read the others.

input_required.why: The input has no value, no default, and isn't optional.
fix: Give the input a value, give it a default, or make it optional: true.

input_condition_not_known.why: An input's hidden:, ignore: or optional: is decided when the run is created, but it reads something that isn't known then, such as a secret.
fix: Make the condition read only inputs and what is known when the run is created.

If the condition reads an input whose value isn't known until the run starts, because its default, or a row's, reads such a thing, make the condition read something else, or make that input's value known when the run is created.

platform_input.why: This type of input names a platform's resources, such as its clusters, and nothing here provides them.
fix: Run the workflow on a platform that provides the input's type.

platform_value_not_json.why: The platform gave a value for the input that a run can't hold, because it isn't JSON. This is a problem in the platform.
fix: Report it to the platform's operators.

input_rejected.why: The platform that provides this input's type rejected its value, for the reason given.
fix: Choose a value the platform has, such as one of its clusters.

input_not_number.why: A number input takes a number, or text that is one.
fix: Submit a number.

input_below_min.why: The input's value is less than the min: its definition gives.
fix: Submit a value at least as large as the minimum.

input_above_max.why: The input's value is more than the max: its definition gives.
fix: Submit a value no larger than the maximum.

input_not_boolean.why: A boolean input takes true or false, or the text "true" or "false".
fix: Submit true or false.

input_not_list.why: A list input takes a list.
fix: Submit a list.

input_not_option_list.why: A multiple-choice dropdown takes a list of its options.
fix: Submit a list of the input's options.

input_not_option.why: A dropdown's value must be one of its options.
fix: Submit one of the options the message lists.

input_not_text.why: A text input takes text, a number or true or false, but not a list or a mapping.
fix: Submit the value as text.

input_looks_secret.why: The input's name, such as api_token, suggests it holds a secret, but it takes text. A text input's value is kept with the run, where whoever can see the run can read it, and isn't masked in the run's logs. A password input's value is a secret: it isn't kept with the run, and is masked. A name looks like a secret's when one of its words, split at _, -, . and changes of case, is a word such as token, password or secret.
fix: If the input holds a secret, give it type: password.

input_too_deep.why: A run's input values are kept with it as JSON, which nests at most 10,000 levels, counting the levels around a value in the run. The limit is Meridian's own, not part of the workflow format.
fix: Give the input a value, or a default, that nests less deeply.

default_row_unknown_input.why: A list's default rows, written in the workflow, have a key that isn't one of the inputs of the list's rows, its template's. The row keeps the value, which what reads the row can read, but it is often a misspelling, or a field the template no longer has. A launch form sends the default rows back, so the key isn't reported again as an unknown input of each run.
fix: Correct the key, add an input of that name to the list's template, or remove the key from the default rows.

duplicate_step_id.why: A step's id names it for the steps after it, so two steps of a job can't share one.
fix: Give one of the steps a different id.

needs_not_known.why: A job's needs: decide the order its jobs run in, so they must be known when the run is created. This needs: reads something that is known only later.
fix: Make needs: read only inputs, variables and what else is known when the run is created.

needs_item_not_name.why: A job's needs: list the names of the jobs it waits for.
fix: List jobs' names.

needs_not_name.why: A job's needs: is the name of the job it waits for, or a list of them.
fix: Write a job's name, or a list of jobs' names.

needs_itself.why: A job can't wait for itself.
fix: Remove the job's own name from its needs:.

needs_unknown_job.why: A job's needs: names a job the workflow doesn't have.
fix: Correct the job's name, or add the job.

needs_cycle.why: These jobs wait for each other, so none of them can start.
fix: Remove one of the needs: that close the cycle.

context_not_known.why: An expression reads a context that isn't known yet where it is evaluated, such as steps in a job's if:, which is decided before its steps run.
fix: Read the value somewhere it is known, or pass it on through an output or env.

status_not_known.why: Status functions such as failure() say how the job or step got here, which isn't known where this expression is evaluated.
fix: Use status functions only in a job's or a step's if:.

relative_outside_definitions.why: A relative reference, such as .name, reads a key beside it in an input's definition. Outside input definitions there is nothing for it to read.
fix: Read the value through its context, such as inputs.name.

undefined_input.why: An expression reads an input the workflow doesn't define, which is null.
fix: Correct the input's name, or define the input.

undefined_nested_input.why: An expression reads an input a group doesn't have, which is null.
fix: Correct the input's name, or add it to the group.

flattened_input_ref.why: A group with flatten: true, and a wizard step unless $meta.wizard.flatten is false, has its inputs' values beside its own, under their own names, as ACTIVATE runs it. So inputs.<group>.<name> doesn't read the input's value, as it doesn't in ACTIVATE.
fix: Read the input by its own name, as inputs.<name>.

needs_outside_job.why: The context needs reads the jobs a job waits for, so it is known only in a job.
fix: Read needs only in a job's keys and steps.

undefined_job.why: An expression reads needs of a job the workflow doesn't have.
fix: Correct the job's name.

job_not_needed.why: A job can read the outputs of the jobs it waits for, and this job doesn't wait for the one it reads.
fix: Add the job it reads to its needs:.

needed_job_no_step.why: An expression reads a step of another job by an id that job's steps don't have.
fix: Correct the step's id, or give the step that id.

needs_unknown_key.why: Each job in needs has outputs, result and steps, and nothing else, so another key reads as the reference's own text, such as needs.build.status, as format 1 reads a word it doesn't know.
fix: Read one of outputs, result or steps.

needs_read_whole.why: Format 1 reads a job in needs by its result, needs.<job>.result, and its outputs and its steps' outputs one by one, by name, as needs.<job>.outputs.<name> and needs.<job>.steps.<id>.outputs.<name>, and any other reference to needs, such as needs.build or needs.build.outputs, as a word it doesn't know: as its own text.
fix: Read each output by its name: needs.<job>.outputs.<name>.

step_not_earlier.why: A step can read the outputs of the steps before it, and this one comes later.
fix: Move the step it reads before this one, or read its outputs later.

undefined_step.why: An expression reads a step by an id no earlier step of the job has.
fix: Correct the step's id, or give the step that id.

output_undefined_step.why: A job's output reads a step by an id none of its steps has. Once the job's steps succeeded, format 1 reads its outputs strictly, so the output fails the job, as one that nothing wrote does (output_not_written); once a step failed or was cancelled, the output is empty.
fix: Correct the step's id, or give the step that id.

steps_unknown_key.why: Each step in steps has outputs, and nothing else, so another key reads as the reference's own text, such as steps.build.result, as format 1 reads a word it doesn't know.
fix: Read steps.<id>.outputs.

output_steps_unknown_key.why: Each step in steps has outputs, and nothing else, so this job output reads another key as the reference's own text, as format 1 reads a word it doesn't know.
fix: Read steps.<id>.outputs.

cleanup_undefined_step.why: A step's cleanup: runs once all of the job's steps have, so it can read the outputs of any of them, its own step's and later ones' among them. It reads a step by an id none of the job's steps has, which is empty.
fix: Correct the step's id, or give the step that id.

cleanup_steps_unknown_key.why: Each step in steps has outputs, and nothing else, so this cleanup: reads another key as the reference's own text, as format 1 reads a word it doesn't know.
fix: Read steps.<id>.outputs.

steps_read_whole.why: Format 1 reads a step's outputs from steps one by one, by name, and any other reference to steps, such as steps.build or steps.build.outputs, as a word it doesn't know: as its own text.
fix: Read each output by its name: steps.<id>.outputs.<name>.

no_matrix.why: The job has no matrix, so matrix.<key> reads as null. ACTIVATE read it as its own text when no job of the workflow had a matrix, which made it depend on the workflow's other jobs.
fix: Give the job a strategy: with a matrix:, or remove the reference.

undefined_matrix_key.why: An expression reads a key the job's matrix doesn't have, which is null.
fix: Correct the key, or add it to the matrix.

undefined_session.why: An expression reads a session the workflow doesn't define.
fix: Correct the session's name, or add it to sessions:.

variable_looks_secret.why: An expression reads an organization or user variable whose name, such as HF_TOKEN, suggests it holds a secret, but it isn't a secret variable. A variable's value is masked in the run's logs only if it is a secret, so a secret in a plain variable shows wherever a step writes it. A name looks like a secret's when one of its words, split at _, -, . and changes of case, is a word such as token, password or secret.
fix: If the variable holds a secret, make it a secret variable.

variable_not_text.why: A variable's value is text. Whoever runs the workflow gave the compiler a value for this variable that is something else, such as a number or a list, which no expression reads as the variable, so the run reads it as "", as it reads a variable that isn't set. As the run starts, Meridian reads each variable again, as text.
fix: Give the variable its value as text, such as "8" rather than 8, or a list as its JSON.

resolver_missing.why: Some of a workflow's keys need what only the place it runs can provide, through one of Meridian's interfaces: sessions: need a session provider (Sessions), a uses: that names a workflow needs a way to fetch it (Sources), and runs-on: execution-group: needs execution groups (Groups). Meridian doesn't run a workflow without what it needs, rather than run part of it.
fix: Run the workflow where the interface is provided, such as on a platform that serves sessions.
Remove the key from the workflow if it doesn't need it.

run_shape_changed.why: What decides a run's shape, which inputs it has and which jobs each job waits for, can read organization and user variables and passwords. The compiler reads them when the run is created, and the plan holds what they decided. As the run starts, Meridian reads them again and decides again, and this decision came out otherwise: a variable or a password changed in between, as one can before a rerun. Rather than run with values from two readings, the run doesn't start.
fix: Create the run again, so that it is created and started with the same values.
If the variable changes often, make the decision read something that doesn't.

values_read_each_other.why: As a run starts, Meridian evaluates the workflow's env: and the inputs whose values it left to the start, in the order they read each other. An input's default can read env, and an env: value an input, but these values read each other, so none of them can be evaluated first.
fix: Change one of the values so that it doesn't read the others.

group_unknown.why: A job's runs-on: execution-group: names an execution group, which runs the job on one of its members. Where the workflow runs, the Groups interface has no group by that name: locally, there is none in groups.yaml, and it isn't the built-in local group.
fix: Name a group that is there, or add the group where the workflow runs, such as to groups.yaml.

environment_unknown.why: A format 1 job's runs-on: environment: names a scheduler environment on a cluster, which only a platform knows. Where the workflow runs, the Groups interface has no such environment: locally there are none.
fix: Run the workflow on the platform that has the environment, or run the job in an execution group instead (runs-on: execution-group:).

source_not_found.why: A step's uses: names a workflow, which is resolved and pinned when the run is created. Where the workflow runs, the Sources interface has no workflow by that reference.
fix: Check the reference: its repository, its revision, and the file its with: $yaml names.

source_not_known.why: The workflow a step's uses: names is resolved and pinned to its commit and its text's digest when the run is created, so that the run and its reruns run the same text. Its uses:, and its with: $yaml and $host, say where it is, so they must be written out, not read from what is known only later. ACTIVATE evaluates them with the run's inputs before it reads them; no known workflow has an expression in one.
fix: Write the reference out in the step's uses:, and the file and the server in its with:.

checkout_not_known.why: A parallelworks/checkout step's repo and branch are pinned to a commit as the run is created, through the Sources interface, so that the coordinator, not the worker, chooses what is fetched, with whose credentials, and so that the run and its reruns check out the same tree. So both must be written out, not read from an expression, as format 1 allows.
fix: Write the repository and the branch out in the step's with:.
To choose among repositories, give each a step of its own, with an if:.

checkout_not_found.why: The Sources interface, which pins a parallelworks/checkout step's repository and branch to a commit as the run is created, found no such revision, without saying why.
fix: Check the repository's URL, and the branch, tag or full commit the step names.

checkout_repo_invalid.why: The coordinator fetches a parallelworks/checkout step's repo, as the run is created, with git and the credentials of whoever runs it, so Meridian takes only an https or ssh URL, or an scp-like one, as user@host:path, on any host, with no credential in it. Another transport, as a local path, file:// or ext::, would have the coordinator read its host's files, or run a command there; git:// and http:// have no TLS or SSH, so nothing fetched would be authenticated; and a user and a password, or a token, in the URL would put a secret in the plan, which everyone who can see the run reads.
fix: Name the repository by an https:// or ssh:// URL, or as user@host:path.
Give git its credential through its own configuration, as a credential helper or an ssh key, rather than in the URL.

checkout_path_invalid.why: Meridian reads each entry of a parallelworks/checkout step's sparse_checkout as a literal path from the repository's root, to a file or a directory, which a slash can end. One that is empty, starts with a slash, holds an empty name, . or .., holds a glob's *, ? or [, starts with !, which format 1 can read as a pattern, or holds a control character, isn't one.
fix: Name each file or directory to check out by its path from the repository's root, with no pattern.

checkout_path_not_found.why: An entry of a parallelworks/checkout step's sparse_checkout names no file and no directory in the commit the step was pinned to as the run was created. Nothing is written for it, as in format 1, and the step goes on.
fix: Check the entry against the repository, at the branch the step names.
Remove an entry the repository no longer has.

checkout_submodules.why: Format 1 clones a whole repository with its submodules. Meridian doesn't fetch submodules yet, so a parallelworks/checkout of a whole repository that has one fails, rather than leave it empty. A sparse checkout leaves submodules empty, as format 1's does.
fix: Check out only the paths the job needs, with sparse_checkout.
Check out a submodule's repository with a step of its own.

checkout_too_large.why: A parallelworks/checkout step's tree reaches the worker from the coordinator, which reads it from the commit the step was pinned to. Meridian bounds the files' sizes, together, in each checkout.
fix: Check out only the paths the job needs, with sparse_checkout.

checkout_too_many.why: A parallelworks/checkout step's tree reaches the worker from the coordinator, which reads it from the commit the step was pinned to. Meridian bounds how many directories, files and links a checkout writes, so that no tree uses up a host's inodes.
fix: Check out only the paths the job needs, with sparse_checkout.

checkout_unavailable.why: The coordinator reads the commit a parallelworks/checkout step was pinned to as the run was created from its copy of the repository, and fetches it again if the copy doesn't have it, 5 times, 2, 4, 8 and 16 seconds apart, as format 1 tries a clone. The repository couldn't be reached, or no longer has the commit, as after a branch was rewritten. The step's retry: can try it again.
fix: Check that the repository can be reached from where Meridian runs, with your credentials.
If the branch was rewritten, run the workflow again, which pins it anew.

checkout_unsafe.why: The worker writes a parallelworks/checkout step's tree only inside the directory the step names, and only what a Git commit holds: directories, files and symbolic links, and no .git, nor a link to one. A member of the tree that is anything else, or whose name leaves that directory, isn't one a commit made, and the step fails before the worker writes it.
fix: Report the bug, with the repository and the commit the step checks out.

checkout_write_failed.why: The worker writes a parallelworks/checkout step's tree into the directory the step names, its path: in its working directory, merging it with what is there, as format 1 copies it: a file of the same name is replaced, and the rest is kept. The system refused one of the writes. The step's retry: can try it again.
fix: Check that the job's user can write to the directory.
Check that the directory has no directory where the tree has a file, and no file where it has a directory.

expression_failed.why: An expression failed in a way Meridian doesn't describe. This is a problem in Meridian.
fix: Report it, with the workflow that causes it.

word_not_reference.why: A word in an expression that looks like a reference is text, because it doesn't start with a context, such as input.name, which is missing the s of inputs.
fix: Correct the context's name, or quote the word if text is what you mean.

hyphenated_name.why: A hyphen in an expression subtracts, as in JavaScript, so a reference to a name with a hyphen in it subtracts its second half, which is NaN.
fix: Read a name with a hyphen in brackets, as in inputs['pw-user'].

condition_word.why: A word in a condition is text, which is always true, so it doesn't decide anything.
fix: Compare the value with what it should be, or use a status function such as failure().

older_always.why: The word always is the older spelling of always(), which runs the job or step whatever happened before it.
fix: Write always().

replaced_keyword.why: The word was once an if: keyword. It is text now, which is always true.
fix: Use the status function the message names.

value_too_deep.why: A run is kept as JSON, which nests at most 10,000 levels. A value counts the levels around it in the run, about as many as the workflow has around it. A mapping whose only key starts with $ counts as two levels, and an expression counts the levels of its parsed form, such as one for each operator, and one for each list or mapping it writes. The limit is Meridian's own, not part of the workflow format.
fix: Nest the value less deeply.

ssh_disconnect_timeout_ignored.why: Format 1 fails a step on a host once its connection to the host has been lost for disconnect-timeout, 300 seconds by default, and never for a negative one. Meridian runs a worker on the host, which goes on running the job's steps while the connection is lost and reports them once it is back, so every step runs as a negative disconnect-timeout asks.
fix: Remove disconnect-timeout, or make it negative, such as -1.
Give the step a timeout: to bound how long it runs.

ssh_disconnect_timeout_invalid.why: Format 1 reads a disconnect-timeout as a number of seconds, or a whole number with one of d, h, m or s after it, such as 300, 5m or -1. It can't read any other, such as 1h30m, 1.5h or 300ms, and fails the step on a host that has one. Meridian doesn't honour the key, so it runs the step all the same.
fix: Remove disconnect-timeout, or write it as format 1 reads it, such as -1 for a step that never gives up on its host.

runs_on_invalid.why: A job's runs-on: picks where it runs, and an expression in it gave something that names no place. runs-on takes an execution group's name, as an execution-groups input gives it; a mapping with execution-group:, or with environment: and its cluster and name; or a compute target, as a compute-target input gives it.
fix: Make the expression give one of these, such as the value of an execution-groups or compute-target input.

resources_invalid.why: A job's resources: says what it needs from where it runs, and each value is read once its expressions are evaluated. cpu is a number of cores, such as 4 or 0.5, or a whole number of thousandths of a core followed by m, such as 500m. memory is a whole number of bytes, or a number followed by a unit: k, M, G, T, P or E for powers of 1000, or Ki, Mi, Gi, Ti, Pi or Ei for powers of 1024. gpu is a whole number. None can be negative.
fix: Give the value in the form the message names.

duration_invalid.why: A timeout or an interval is a duration: a whole number of seconds, such as 300, or a whole number followed by s for seconds, m for minutes, h for hours or d for days, such as 10m. An expression in it gave something else.
fix: Make the expression give a duration in that form.

count_invalid.why: How many times a job or a step may run again is a number. A number is taken, and so is text that reads as one, such as an output; a fraction is rounded down, and a negative number is 0. An expression in it gave something else.
fix: Make the expression give a number.

matrix_not_list.why: Each key of a matrix other than include and exclude lists the values the job runs with, and include and exclude list entries. An expression gave something that isn't a list for one of them.
fix: Make the expression give a list, such as a list input's value or a range of numbers.

matrix_entry_not_mapping.why: Each entry of a matrix's include and exclude is a mapping of matrix keys to values: an exclude entry removes the combinations that have all its values, and an include entry adds its values to the combinations it matches, or is a combination of its own.
fix: Write each entry as a mapping.

matrix_empty.why: A matrix job runs once for each combination of its matrix's values. This matrix has none: a key lists no values, or exclude removes every combination, and include adds none.
fix: Give each key at least one value, or remove the exclude entries that remove every combination.

matrix_too_large.why: Meridian runs a matrix of at most a limit of combinations, 256 unless whoever runs the workflow sets another. It also stops counting a matrix's combinations once it has looked at about 16 million of them and of the exclude entries it checks them against, so a matrix far larger than the limit before its exclude entries remove most of it is too large as well. The limits are Meridian's own, not part of the workflow format.
fix: Make the matrix smaller, or ask whoever runs the workflow for a higher limit.

output_not_written.why: Format 1 reads a job's output, needs.<job>.outputs.<name>, and a step's, steps.<id>.outputs.<name>, strictly where a job or a step is about to run, and in a job's outputs: once its steps succeeded: one that nothing wrote fails what reads it, rather than read as "", so that a command such as rm -rf with an empty path never runs. A step's cleanup:, a step or a job whose if: is the word always, and an if: itself, read it as "".
fix: Write the output in the step or job that the expression reads, or read it with a default, such as needs.<job>.outputs.<name> || 'value', in a step whose if: is always.

working_directory_variable.why: A working directory is used as it is, and no shell expands the variables in it, so $HOME or ${PW_JOB_DIR} would be a directory of that name. Format 1 fails the step instead.
fix: Read the value with an expression, such as env.PW_JOB_DIR, or write the path out.

job_ssh_host_empty.why: A format 1 job's ssh: runs the job's steps on the host its remoteHost names. One that is empty or null names none, and format 1 runs the job where it would run without an ssh:, with a note in each step's log, which is often a mistake, such as an input left empty. Meridian runs it there too, and keeps this warning with the job.
fix: Give the ssh: a remoteHost, or remove it to run the job where it runs without one.

undefined_env.why: env holds what the workflow's, the job's and the step's env: define, and the variables format 1 gives a step, such as PW_JOB_DIR and OUTPUTS. A name none of them defines reads as "", whatever the environment the step runs in holds, since an expression is evaluated before the step runs. A job's env:, working-directory: and outputs: read only the variables format 1 gives as the job starts, such as PW_JOB_DIR, and not those it gives a step alone, such as OUTPUTS and PW_WORKFLOW_STEP_CURRENT_RETRY.
fix: Define the variable in an env:, or read it in the step's script, as $NAME.
Write an expression, or remove the ${{ }}.

expression_too_deep.why: The expression nests more deeply than the limit, which keeps evaluating it bounded.
fix: Split it into simpler expressions.

expression_ends_early.why: The expression stops before it is complete, such as after an operator.
fix: Finish the expression.

unexpected_text.why: The expression has text where it can't be read, such as two values with no operator between them.
fix: Check the expression near the text the message names.

ternary_missing_colon.why: A condition ? a : b needs its :.
fix: Add the : and the value for when the condition is false.

coalesce_mixed.why: As in JavaScript, ?? can't be mixed with || or && without parentheses, because which is evaluated first isn't clear.
fix: Add parentheses, as the message shows.

invalid_json_literal.why: Lists and mappings in an expression are written in JSON, which has double quotes and no trailing commas.
fix: Write the list or mapping in JSON.

not_a_function.why: The expression calls a name that isn't one of the functions expressions have. Function names are case-sensitive.
fix: Correct the function's name.

call_missing_comma.why: A call's arguments are separated by commas and end with ).
fix: Add the missing , or ).

wrong_argument_count.why: The function is called with a different number of arguments than it takes.
fix: Call it with the number of arguments the message names.

case_arguments.why: The function case() takes pairs of a condition and a value, then the value for when no condition holds.
fix: Give case() an odd number of arguments, ending with the default.

expected_close_paren.why: A parenthesis is opened and never closed.
fix: Add the missing ).

unclosed_string.why: A quoted string doesn't end before the expression does.
fix: Add the closing quote.

unclosed_bracket.why: A bracket is opened and never closed.
fix: Add the closing bracket.

unclosed_template.why: A ${{ starts an expression, which needs a }} to end it.
fix: Add the }}, or write ${{ '${{' }} where the text ${{ is meant.

lambda_expected.why: The functions map() and filter() take a list, then a lambda that they run for each item, such as x => x + 1. A lambda is a parameter, or one or two in parentheses, then => and its body.
fix: Write the last argument as a lambda, such as h => h.name.

lambda_too_many_parameters.why: A lambda of map() or filter() takes the item, and optionally its index in a list or its key in a mapping, as in (h, i) => i.
fix: Remove the parameters after the second.

lambda_parameter_reserved.why: A lambda's parameter can't take a name that already means something in an expression: a context, such as inputs; the keywords true, false, null and undefined, and the operators and and or, in any case; a word operator, such as in or length; NaN and Infinity, in any case; or index, which [index] reads.
fix: Give the parameter another name, such as item.

lambda_parameter_twice.why: A lambda's parameters are the item and its index or key, so each needs its own name. As in JavaScript, a lambda can't give two parameters the same name.
fix: Rename one of them, as in (h, i) => i.

lambda_misplaced.why: A lambda, written with =>, can only be the last argument of map() or filter(), which run it for each item. Anywhere else, => isn't part of an expression.
fix: Move the lambda into map() or filter(), after the list it goes through.

format_unclosed_brace.why: The template of format() has a { that doesn't close. Write {{ for a literal {.
fix: Close the placeholder, or write {{ for a literal {.

format_missing_argument.why: The template of format() has a placeholder, such as {1}, with no argument for it.
fix: Add the argument, or remove the placeholder.

format_unopened_brace.why: The template of format() has a } that no { opens. Write }} for a literal }.
fix: Remove the }, or write }} for a literal }.

range_not_whole.why: The range operator makes a list of whole numbers, so it takes whole numbers.
fix: Round the numbers, such as with round or floor.

range_out_of_bounds.why: The range operator takes numbers a JavaScript number holds exactly, from -2^53 to 2^53.
fix: Use smaller numbers.

range_too_long.why: The range operator makes a list of at most 10,000 numbers.
fix: Make the range shorter.

from_json_invalid.why: The function fromJSON reads JSON, and the text it was given isn't.
fix: Check the text it reads, such as a step's output.

unknown_operator.why: A stored expression uses an operator this version of Meridian doesn't have.
fix: Compile the workflow again with this version.

expression_too_large.why: The expressions in one string build more text and lists than the language allows a string, 8 MiB, a limit that keeps evaluating them bounded.
fix: Build less, such as by reading part of a value rather than all of it.

expression_too_much_work.why: The expressions in one string do more work than the language allows a string, 32 MiB, a limit that keeps evaluating them bounded. Work is counted in bytes: 8 for each step, such as an operand, an operator, a call or a run of a lambda, plus the size of each value that an operation such as == or keys reads, plus what the expressions build.
fix: Do less work, such as by going through part of a list rather than all of it, or by reading less of a large value in each lambda.

expressions_read_each_other.why: Expressions in the workflow read each other's values, so none of them can be evaluated first.
fix: Change one of them so that it doesn't read the others.

not_list_or_mapping.why: The functions map() and filter() go through a list's items, or a mapping's values in the order of their keys. A string that holds a JSON list or mapping is read as its value, and null has no items. Anything else, such as a number or other text, is an error.
fix: Check the value of the first argument, such as an input or a step's output.

expressions_build_too_much.why: Meridian evaluates some expressions together, and bounds what they build between them as well as what each one builds. Each of these is within the language's limit, but together they build more than Meridian allows. The limit is Meridian's own, not part of the workflow format. The expressions evaluated together are a run's input defaults and conditions with its jobs' needs:, or the templates in one value, such as a step's with:.
fix: Build less in these expressions, such as by reading part of a value rather than all of it.

expressions_too_much_work.why: Meridian evaluates some expressions together, and bounds the work they do between them as well as the work each one does. Each of these is within the language's limit, but together they do more than Meridian allows. The limit is Meridian's own, not part of the workflow format. The expressions evaluated together are a run's input defaults and conditions with its jobs' needs:, or the templates in one value, such as a step's with:.
fix: Do less work in these expressions, such as by going through part of a list rather than all of it.

expressions_too_slow.why: Meridian evaluates some expressions together, and stops them once evaluating them has taken 10 seconds between them. This is a safeguard behind the language's limit on the work each expression does, and Meridian's on the work they do together, against workflows that do far more than any real one. It isn't a limit of the workflow format, since how long evaluating takes depends on the machine. The expressions evaluated together are a run's input defaults and conditions with its jobs' needs:, or the templates in one value, such as a step's with:.
fix: Do less work in these expressions, such as by going through part of a list rather than all of it, or by reading less of a large value in each lambda.

problems_not_listed.why: Meridian lists at most the first 100 problems of each kind that it finds in a workflow and the values submitted for a run, so that a workflow or values with very many of them don't make a list of problems, or a plan, as large. The rest of the kind are counted here instead.
fix: Fix the problems that are listed, and check the workflow again to see the rest.

container_not_supported.why: A job's steps run in a container when the member it was placed on isolates jobs in one, as local and ssh members do by default. This version of Meridian's worker runs steps only on the host. Meridian never runs a job with weaker isolation than its member asks for, so the attempt fails before any step runs, and the job is placed again, on another member of its group if there is one.
fix: Name host isolation in the settings of the members the job runs on, if running its steps on the host is what you want.

job_unreadable.why: A worker reads the job it claims as strictly as a plan is read, and refuses one with a part it doesn't know, rather than run the job without it. This happens when the worker and the coordinator are from versions of Meridian that encode a job differently. No step ran, so the job is placed again.
fix: Start workers of the same version of Meridian as the coordinator.

job_version_unsupported.why: A worker claims a job with the newest plan version it reads, and the coordinator sends it a job of that version. One of another version means the coordinator didn't honour that, as a coordinator of another version of Meridian might not. No step ran, so the job is placed again.
fix: Start workers of the same version of Meridian as the coordinator.

run_dir_unusable.why: Each run has a directory, PW_JOB_DIR, where its steps run by default. The worker makes it if it doesn't exist, and if it can't, for the reason given, the attempt fails before any step runs. The job is placed again, on another member of its group if there is one.
fix: Check that the user the job runs as can make the directory, and write to it, on the host the job was placed on.

env_name_invalid.why: A platform gives a job's steps variables of its own, such as PW_USER, in the attempt's claim. The worker sets each in a step's environment, where a name can't be empty or hold = or NUL, so it refuses the attempt before any step runs, rather than run the steps without the variable. The job is placed again, on another member of its group if there is one.
fix: Report it to whoever runs the platform: the platform gave the variable.

uses_not_supported.why: A step that uses: an action, such as parallelworks/checkout, or a workflow runs it rather than a command. This version of Meridian's worker runs only steps with run:, so the step fails.
fix: Do the step's work with a run: command instead.

action_needs_platform.why: parallelworks/scheduler-agent starts a platform's agent on a cluster's compute node, through the cluster's scheduler, with the platform's command-line tool and credentials, and parallelworks/wait-for-agent waits for it. Each needs the platform that provides it, which Meridian, run on its own, doesn't have, so a step that uses one fails when it runs, as a step whose command fails does: its retry: tries it again, its ignore-errors: lets its last try succeed, and its cleanup: runs. It fails only then: a step that its if: skips, or that is in a job its if: skips, never runs, and the run doesn't fail for it, so Meridian doesn't refuse such a workflow when it creates its run.
fix: Skip the step, or its job, where no platform provides the action, with an if: that reads an input, such as one that says whether to use the scheduler's agent.
Run the workflow on the platform that provides the action.

action_request_failed.why: A step that uses a built-in action the coordinator performs, such as parallelworks/cancel-jobs, asks the coordinator for it, through the worker API, and the coordinator answers how the action ended. That request failed for good: the coordinator refused it, or answered with what the worker can't read, which the reason names by its code. That is a bug in the worker or in the coordinator, or a worker and a coordinator of releases that don't agree on the worker API, and not the workflow's. The step fails, and isn't tried again. If the coordinator answered, it may have performed the action, as its record of the run says.
fix: Start workers of the coordinator's own release of Meridian.
If they are of the same release, report the bug, with the reason and the worker's log.

child_request_failed.why: A step whose uses: names a workflow asks the coordinator, through the worker API, for the run of it, waits for that run's end, and stops it when the step is stopped. One of those requests failed for good: the coordinator refused it, or answered with what the worker can't read, which the reason names by its code. That is a bug in the worker or in the coordinator, or a worker and a coordinator of releases that don't agree on the worker API, and not the workflow's. The step fails, and isn't tried again. The run it calls may have been created, and may still be running: its own status says.
fix: Start workers of the coordinator's own release of Meridian.
If they are of the same release, report the bug, with the reason and the worker's log.

child_dir_unusable.why: A run that a step calls has a directory of its own, subworkflows/<job>/step_<n> under the step's working directory, as in format 1, where its steps run. The worker that runs the step makes it before it asks for the run, a directory at a time from its root run's directory, and never follows a symbolic link on the way, which one of the run's own steps could have left there to put the called workflow somewhere else: a link is refused as too many levels of symbolic links, and a file that isn't a directory as not a directory. With clean-on-retry:, which is true unless the workflow says otherwise, the worker removes the directory, with what it holds, before each try after the first, and never follows a link there either. The step fails, and isn't tried again.
fix: Remove the symbolic link, or the file, that the reason names, or have the run's steps not make one there.
Check that the user the job runs as can make the directory, and write to it, on the host the job was placed on.

cancel_jobs_job_unknown.why: A parallelworks/cancel-jobs step's jobs: names the jobs of its run to cancel. This name is no job of the run, or is a matrix job's, whose instances format 1 knows by other names, so that it cancels none of them. As in format 1, the step does nothing for the name, and succeeds.
fix: Correct the job's name, or take it out of jobs:.

cancel_jobs_other_run.why: With slug, workflow and run, or run alone, a parallelworks/cancel-jobs step cancels jobs of another run, in format 1. Meridian doesn't do that yet, so the step fails when it runs, as a step whose command fails does: its retry: tries it again, and its ignore-errors: lets its last try succeed. It fails only then: an if: can skip it.
fix: Leave out slug, workflow and run, to cancel jobs of the step's own run.
Cancel the other run itself, as with meridian cancel.

cancel_jobs_run_missing.why: A parallelworks/cancel-jobs step's with: names a run to cancel by its workflow and its number, as format 1 reads them: a workflow without a run, or with a negative one, names none, and format 1 fails the step, as Meridian does.
fix: Give run: the run's number, with the workflow:.
Leave out workflow:, to cancel jobs of the step's own run.

step_ssh_not_supported.why: A format 1 step's ssh: runs the step on another host over SSH. This version of Meridian's worker runs steps only on the host it runs on, so the step fails rather than run on the wrong host.
fix: Move the step to a job that runs on that host, through the job's ssh: or an execution group.

step_off_job_host.why: A format 1 job's ssh: runs its steps on the host it names, and a step's ssh: that is null, or gives no remoteHost, runs the step where the job would run without its ssh:. This version of Meridian's worker runs on the job's host, and runs steps only there, so the step fails rather than run on the wrong host.
fix: Move the step to a job that runs where the step should, such as one without an ssh:.
Remove the step's ssh: to run it on the job's host.

ssh_host_empty.why: A format 1 step's ssh: runs the step on the host its remoteHost names. One that is empty or null names none, and format 1 runs the step where it would run without an ssh:, with a note in its log, which is often a mistake, such as an input left empty.
fix: Give the ssh: a remoteHost, or remove it to run the step where its job runs.

step_not_started.why: The worker writes the step's command to a script, and starts the step's shell with it in the step's working directory, which it makes if it doesn't exist. That failed, for the reason given, so the command never ran.
fix: Check that the step's shell is on the host, and that its working directory can be made there.

evaluation_failed.why: The worker evaluates a job's env: as the job starts, each step as it is about to run, and the job's outputs once its steps have run. One of these failed with an error of Meridian's own, not a problem with the workflow, so the step, or the job, failed.
fix: Report the bug, with the worker's log, which records the error.

worker_dir_unusable.why: A worker keeps a step's script and $OUTPUTS in a directory of its own, which only you can use, and makes another if a step removes it: in the same place, or else in the next it would have used, of meridian/worker in your cache directory, XDG_RUNTIME_DIR and the system's temporary directory. It could make one in none of them, so the step didn't start. The code is the problem with the first of them, and its page says why.
fix: Fix what the code's page says, for the directory the message names, or set XDG_RUNTIME_DIR to a directory only you can change.

shell_not_supported.why: Format 1 runs a step's command with bash or sh only, as its shell: says, so the step fails without running. The workflow's schema allows no other shell, so this happens only for a plan made without checking it.
fix: Run the step with bash or sh, by name or path, as in shell: bash -l {0}.

step_timed_out.why: A step's timeout:, and its retry:'s timeout for each try, limit how long it runs. The worker sends a step that runs past one SIGTERM, then SIGKILL if it hasn't ended after a grace period. A step that ran past its own timeout: isn't tried again; a try past its retry:'s timeout is, while the step has retries left.
fix: Raise the timeout, or make the step finish sooner.

outputs_too_large.why: A job's outputs are kept with its run and given to the jobs that need it, so Meridian limits each file of outputs that a step writes, the file $OUTPUTS names, to 1 MiB, counting each byte that isn't UTF-8 as the 3 bytes of the U+FFFD that replaces it. The limit is Meridian's own, not part of the workflow format.
fix: Write large results to a file in the run's directory, and give its path as the output.

outputs_line_too_long.why: Format 1 reads $OUTPUTS a line at a time, and reads none of a file with a line of 64 KiB or longer. Meridian reads it the same way, so that a workflow means what it did. The steps without an id share their job's file, so a long line there also hides what the steps after it write.
fix: Write large values to a file in the run's directory, and give its path as the output.

outputs_not_utf8.why: A step's outputs reach the coordinator, and the jobs that need the job, as JSON, as format 1 stores them, and JSON holds only UTF-8 text. So, as format 1 does, the worker replaces each byte of an output's name or value that isn't UTF-8 with U+FFFD, the replacement character, and the jobs that need the job read that in its place. Text in another encoding, such as Latin-1, has such bytes, and so has binary data. The step's log keeps what it printed as it printed it.
fix: Convert text to UTF-8 before writing it to $OUTPUTS, as iconv -t UTF-8 does.
Write binary data as base64, or to a file in the run's directory, and give its path as the output.

outputs_not_file.why: The worker reads a step's outputs from the file $OUTPUTS names, or from what a symbolic link there names, as format 1 does. It reads only a regular file, opened without waiting, so that a FIFO there can't make it wait forever; the step put something else there, so its outputs can't be read, and it fails. Format 1 waits forever instead, which is a bug. The worker puts a file there again for the steps after it.
fix: Write outputs to $OUTPUTS with >>, or make it a link to a regular file.

outputs_removed.why: The worker keeps $OUTPUTS in a directory of its own, which no other user can change, and reads it once the step ends. Something removed that directory while the step ran: the step itself, or another of your processes, such as a cleaner of temporary files. The worker doesn't trust what is at its path after that, so it doesn't read what the step wrote there.
fix: Don't remove the directory $OUTPUTS is in, or what holds it.

log_not_kept.why: While the coordinator can't be reached, the worker keeps running the job's steps, and keeps their logs on disk to send once it can, up to a limit. Past the limit, or once the disk is full, it doesn't keep what the steps print, so the log is missing that much of it.
fix: Check the connection between the host the job ran on and the coordinator, and the space on the disk that holds the worker's directory, as TMPDIR does by default.

report_not_encoded.why: The worker reports each step's events, and the job's end, to the coordinator as JSON. It couldn't encode one of them, as one holding text that isn't UTF-8, which is a bug in the worker: it replaces such bytes in a step's outputs. Rather than stop the attempt, which the coordinator would take for a lost worker, it sent the report without its outputs and problems, and failed the job, unless it was cancelled, so that no job that needs it reads outputs that are missing. The worker's log says what it couldn't encode.
fix: Report the bug, with the worker's log.

record_unreadable.why: A run's secret record holds what the run was given and the secrets it read. It is encrypted with AES-256-GCM under a data key of the run's own, bound to the run's ID, to its store's, and to how many times it has been encrypted again, so that it can't be moved to another run, even one of the same workflow with the same inputs, nor to a run with the same ID in another store, nor be put back in the place of a later record of its run. This one doesn't decrypt as its run's latest: it was moved from another run or another store, an older one was put back, or it was changed. Rather than run with what another run was given, or with what its own run had before, the run fails.
fix: Rerun the run, which makes its secret record again from what is submitted.
Find out what changed the store's database: Meridian writes a run's secret record for that run alone.

record_reseal_limit.why: A run's secret record is encrypted again under the same data key, with a new random nonce, each time the run adds to it, as when a job ends with private outputs. A data key is used a limited number of times, so that two of its nonces are never likely to be the same, which would weaken the encryption. This run has added to its record that many times, and it fails rather than go past the limit.
fix: If the run has that many jobs and matrix instances with private outputs, split it into several runs.
Otherwise report it as a bug: no run with fewer jobs adds to its record that often.

run_record_mismatch.why: A run's secret record holds what the run was given, and names the plan it was made with. As the run starts, Meridian checks that the record fits the plan: that it names the plan by its digest, and holds what the plan says it holds. This one doesn't, as when a record or a plan was changed in the store, or written by a release that made them otherwise. Rather than start with values that don't belong to its plan, the run fails.
fix: Rerun the run, which makes its plan and its secret record again from the workflow and what is submitted.

run_start_unanswered.why: As a run starts, Meridian reads the organization and user variables it needs, and asks the platform again about the inputs of its types. One of them couldn't answer each time Meridian tried, as when a service it reaches is down. Meridian tries again a few times, waiting longer each time, and then fails the run rather than leave it waiting.
fix: Check that what the run reads as it starts can be reached, such as the platform's services, then rerun the run.

run_malformed.why: Meridian stores a run's plan and its secret record encoded in the version of plans the run was created with, which they name. This run's plan or record names no version, or names one this release reads but doesn't decode as it: it was changed in the store, or written by a release with a fault.
fix: Rerun the run.
Find out what changed the store's database.

run_not_started.why: Each run starts with a step of the coordinator's own, which reads what the run needs and stores what it gives. The coordinator tried that step again and again and failed each time, as when its store can't be written, so it ended the run rather than leave it waiting.
fix: Check the coordinator's log for why it couldn't start the run, then rerun the run.

run_plan_newer.why: A run's plan is versioned, and a release of Meridian starts only runs whose plans are of a version it reads. A newer release created this run, so Meridian leaves it as it is, for a release that reads its plan.
fix: Start the run with the release of Meridian that created it, or a later one.

log_cut.why: A step's log is stored as its worker uploads it, and the worker uploads all of it before it reports the attempt's end. This attempt ended otherwise: its worker was lost, as when its host went away, or a newer attempt of its job took its place, or its placement was withdrawn. What the worker hadn't uploaded by then isn't stored, and never will be: the log is shown as far as it was stored.
fix: See why the attempt ended in the run's events, and on the host the job ran on: its worker's own log, and the step's output if it wrote any to a file of its own, are there.

log_truncated.why: A step's log is stored by the coordinator as the worker uploads it. So that a job that prints without end can't fill the coordinator's disk, the coordinator keeps the bytes of an attempt's logs up to a limit on all of them together. A log that goes past it keeps its bytes to there, then this line, and nothing more of it, and the attempt's later logs keep only this line. The steps run on, and the worker is told the rest is stored.
fix: Have the step print less, or write what it makes to a file of its own, in the run's directory, rather than to its output.

placement_impossible.why: Before a job runs, Meridian asks each member of its execution group whether it can run it: whether it is healthy, and has what the job asks for, within its longest walltime. None of them can, and each member's reason follows this one.
fix: Fix what each member's reason says, such as by asking for fewer resources or a shorter timeout:, or run the job in a group with a member that can run it, then rerun the run.

placement_unanswered.why: To place a job, Meridian asks the backends of its group's members, such as a scheduler over SSH, whether they can run it, and has one start its worker. They couldn't answer each time Meridian asked, as when a host can't be reached. Meridian asks again a few times, waiting longer each time, and then counts it as a failure before the job's first step: it places the job again a while later, and the second time fails it, with setup_failed.
fix: Check that the group's members can be reached, and the coordinator's log for why they couldn't answer, then rerun the run.

setup_failed.why: Each attempt of a job starts a worker, which sets the job up before its first step runs: it makes the run's directory, starts the job's container, and checks that it is the worker Meridian placed. A failure there runs none of the workflow's code, so Meridian places the job again, a few times, waiting longer each time. It fails the job after the fourth such failure, or after the second with the same reason, which follows this one.
fix: Fix what the last failure's reason says, then rerun the run.

coordinator_job_failed.why: Meridian's coordinator sees each job from the moment it is ready to its end. It couldn't for this job: it failed again and again, as when its store can't be written, or the job's placement was withdrawn. So it ended the job as failed rather than leave it waiting.
fix: Check the coordinator's log for what kept it from running the job, then rerun the run.

worker_lost.why: A worker is lost when its backend says it has ended without completing its attempt, or, for a job whose retry: lists worker-lost, once it hasn't renewed its lease for the lease and a margin after it. Once a step has started, the workflow's code may have run, and Meridian runs a job again only when its retry: lists worker-lost, which this job's doesn't.
fix: Find out why the worker ended, as from its node or its scheduler, which the run's log of the attempt names.
If the job is safe to run again from its first step, give it retry: with reasons: [worker-lost], and rerun the run.

worker_lost_again.why: The job's retry: lists worker-lost, so Meridian ran it again each time its worker was lost after a step had started, up to its max-retries, and its worker was lost once more.
fix: Find out why its workers keep ending, as from their nodes or their scheduler.
Or raise the job's max-retries, and rerun the run.

worker_ended_early.why: The worker's backend says the worker ended before the job's first step started, so none of the workflow's code ran. That counts as a failure before the first step: Meridian places the job again, and fails it after a few such failures, or after the second for the same reason.
fix: Look at the worker's log on its member, as its backend keeps it, for why it ended.

worker_killed.why: The worker's backend says its scheduler, or the kernel, ended the worker: at the job's time limit, or for using more memory than the job may. Meridian doesn't run the job again for that.
fix: Give the job a longer timeout:, or more memory with resources:, or make it need less, and rerun the run.

member_gone.why: Meridian asks a member's backend whether an attempt's worker still runs once the attempt's lease lapses, or before its worker has claimed it. The member the attempt was placed on is no longer in its group, as after the group was changed in the config, so its backend can't be asked. Once the grace has passed, Meridian takes the worker for lost: if no step had started, that is a failure before the first step, and the job is placed again on a member its group has; otherwise the job fails, or runs again if its retry: lists worker-lost.
fix: Put the member back in the group while it has workers running, or let the job be placed again.

job_timeout_enforced.why: The worker enforces a job's timeout: itself. As a backstop for one that doesn't, the coordinator waits the job's timeout, the worker's time to stop its steps, a heartbeat period and a margin after the attempt was claimed; then it tells the worker to stop the job, and once its lease lapses without the job's end, withdraws its placement and fails the job with the reason timeout.
fix: Give the job a timeout: long enough for its steps, or make them finish sooner.
If the worker didn't stop the job at its timeout, look at its log on its member for why.

workflow_too_large.why: A workflow file is read whole, so there is a limit on its size. This one came from a stream, such as standard input, which Meridian stopped reading once it passed the limit.
fix: Move long scripts out of the workflow, into files the steps run.
Check that the stream is the workflow you meant, and not a device or a pipe that never ends.

execution_group_unknown.why: An execution-groups input's value is the name of one of the execution groups of the person running the workflow. On their own machine, those are the built-in local group and the groups of groups.yaml in Meridian's config directory.
fix: Choose one of the groups the message lists.
Or define the group in groups.yaml in Meridian's config directory.

cluster_unknown.why: A compute-clusters input's value names a cluster, and the run sees the cluster's details, such as its ip and its schedulerType. On the machine running the workflow, a name is the workspace, this machine, as workspace or user-workspace, or one of the clusters of clusters.yaml in Meridian's config directory, whatever the input's include-workspace, provider and csp say, which only choose what a form lists.
fix: Choose one of the clusters the message lists, or the workspace.
Or define the cluster in clusters.yaml in Meridian's config directory, with the SSH host that reaches it.

clusters_none.why: A compute-clusters input's value names a cluster. On the machine running the workflow, a name is the workspace, this machine, as workspace or user-workspace, or one of the clusters of clusters.yaml in Meridian's config directory, and there is no clusters.yaml, or it defines no cluster.
fix: Define the cluster in clusters.yaml in Meridian's config directory, with the SSH host that reaches it.
Or run the workflow on a platform that provides the input's clusters.

source_ref_invalid.why: Meridian reads a workflow that a step's uses: names from a Git repository, as ACTIVATE does: github/ and the repository's owner and name, or gitlab/ and a project's path, its groups' names among it, and then @ and a branch, tag or commit, the default branch unless it names one. The workflow's file in the repository is the step's with: $yaml, workflow.yaml unless it names another, and with: $host names a GitLab server, only for gitlab/. A part that could be read as something else, such as .. in a path or a revision that starts with -, isn't allowed, nor is a group's name that ends in .git or .lock.
fix: Write the reference as github/<owner>/<repository>@<revision>, or gitlab/<group>/<project>@<revision>, with the workflow's file in with: $yaml.

source_on_platform.why: A uses: that starts with marketplace/ or workflow/ names a workflow that a platform, such as ACTIVATE, keeps. Meridian on its own reads workflows from Git repositories.
fix: Run the workflow on the platform that stores the workflow it uses.
Or name the workflow by its Git repository, as github/<owner>/<repository>@<revision>, with its file in with: $yaml.

source_revision_not_found.why: Meridian fetches the revision a uses: names with git, and git found no such repository, or no such branch, tag or commit in it. A private repository that git can't read with your credentials can look the same.
fix: Check the repository's owner and name, and the revision after @. Git fetches a commit by its full SHA, of 40 or 64 characters, where ACTIVATE takes a short one too.
Check that git can fetch the repository with your credentials, as with git ls-remote and the repository's URL.

source_file_not_found.why: A uses: names a file in the repository, workflow.yaml unless it names another, and the commit its revision names has no file of that name. A directory isn't a workflow file.
fix: Check the path in the reference, after the repository's name.
Check that the revision has the file: the default branch may not.

source_too_large.why: Meridian reads a workflow that a step uses whole, so it limits its size, as it does any workflow's.
fix: Check that the reference names a workflow file, and not another file in the repository.
Split the workflow into smaller ones that call each other with uses:.

source_changed.why: A run pins each workflow its steps use to a commit and the SHA-256 digest of its text, so that the run and its reruns run the same code. The text at that commit has another digest, which can only happen if the repository's history or Meridian's copy of it was changed.
fix: Don't rerun the run. Start a new one, which pins the workflow again.
Find out who could change the repository's history or Meridian's cache directory.

source_not_pinned.why: A run reads each workflow its steps use by the commit and the digest it was pinned to when the run was created, never by a branch that may have moved. This one's record is missing one of them.
fix: Start a new run, which pins the workflow again.

directory_variable_relative.why: MERIDIAN_CONFIG_DIR, MERIDIAN_STATE_DIR and MERIDIAN_CACHE_DIR choose Meridian's directories. Each must be an absolute path, so that the directory it names doesn't depend on where Meridian runs from.
fix: Set the variable to an absolute path, or unset it.

home_unknown.why: Meridian keeps its config, state and cache in directories in your home directory, unless MERIDIAN_CONFIG_DIR, MERIDIAN_STATE_DIR and MERIDIAN_CACHE_DIR choose others.
fix: Set HOME to your home directory.
Or set the variable the message names to an absolute path.

directory_unavailable.why: Meridian creates its state and cache directories when it first needs them, and a worker the directory it keeps its own files in, and the operating system refused or failed.
fix: Fix what the reason names, such as a parent directory you can't write to.
Or choose another directory with MERIDIAN_STATE_DIR or MERIDIAN_CACHE_DIR, or, for a worker, set XDG_RUNTIME_DIR to one only you can change.

not_a_directory.why: Meridian keeps its config, state and cache in directories, and a worker its own files, and something else is at the path it would use for one.
fix: Move what is at the path, or choose another directory with MERIDIAN_CONFIG_DIR, MERIDIAN_STATE_DIR or MERIDIAN_CACHE_DIR, or, for a worker, set XDG_RUNTIME_DIR to one only you can change.

directory_not_owned.why: Meridian's directories hold your config, the key that wraps your runs' secrets, your logs and copies of private repositories, and a worker's its steps' scripts and outputs. A directory another user owns is one they can change.
fix: Choose a directory of your own with MERIDIAN_CONFIG_DIR, MERIDIAN_STATE_DIR or MERIDIAN_CACHE_DIR, or, for a worker, set XDG_RUNTIME_DIR to one only you can change.

directory_not_private.why: Meridian's state directory holds the key that wraps your runs' secrets, its cache directory copies of repositories that may be private, and a worker's directory its steps' scripts, which can hold secrets, so only you may read them; and no one else may change a directory a worker makes its own in. Meridian doesn't tighten a directory that was open, since what was in it may have been read already.
fix: Run chmod 700 on the directory, once you're sure nothing in it was read or changed.
Or choose a new directory with MERIDIAN_STATE_DIR or MERIDIAN_CACHE_DIR, or, for a worker, set XDG_RUNTIME_DIR to one only you can change.

path_unsafe.why: A user who can change a directory on the way to one of Meridian's could replace what is in it with their own after Meridian checked it. As OpenSSH does, Meridian accepts a directory on the way only if it belongs to you or to root and only you or root can change it, or if its sticky bit stops other users removing what isn't theirs, as /tmp's does, and what follows it is yours.
fix: Choose a directory whose parents only you or root can change, such as one in your home directory, or one that mktemp -d -p /var/tmp makes.
Or have the directory's owner run chmod go-w on it.

If it is the directory meridian run makes runs' directories in, under the system's temporary directory, which another user can make first, set TMPDIR to a directory of your own, or name the run's directory with --run-dir.

network_filesystem.why: SQLite's locks don't work reliably on network filesystems, which is where home directories on clusters often are, so Meridian won't keep its database there. It takes every FUSE filesystem, and every folder a virtual machine shares with its host, as Docker Desktop's bind mounts are, for one too, since whether their locks hold can't be told.
fix: Set MERIDIAN_STATE_DIR to a directory on a local disk that only you can change, and that lasts: it holds the database and the key that wraps your runs' secrets, which are lost with it. One that mktemp -d -p /var/tmp makes will do, or one on the node's persistent local disk, but not one in /tmp, which a reboot can empty.

filesystem_unknown.why: Meridian checks that its database's directory isn't on a network filesystem before it opens the database, and the operating system didn't say.
fix: Fix what the reason names, or choose another directory with MERIDIAN_STATE_DIR.

file_unreadable.why: Meridian needs to read the file, and the operating system refused or failed.
fix: Fix what the reason names, such as a path that doesn't exist or a file you can't read.

file_not_regular.why: Meridian reads its config, its key, variables' values and a worker's bootstrap token only from regular files, so that reading one can't wait forever on a pipe or read from a device, and never through a symbolic link at the file's own path, so that what it reads is the file the path names: a directory on the way to it can be a link.
fix: Put the file itself at its path, rather than a link to it: the directory that holds it can be a link instead.

file_not_owned.why: A user who owns one of Meridian's files, or a file that holds a variable's value, can change what it holds, such as where your jobs run, or the key that protects your runs' secrets.
fix: Replace the file with one of your own.

file_not_private.why: The file holds a secret, or what protects them: the key that wraps your runs' secret records, the variables file, since people keep secrets in plain variables too, or a secret variable's value. Only you may read it.
fix: Run chmod 600 on the file.

file_changeable.why: A user who could change your groups or a variable's value could send your jobs where they choose, or choose what your jobs read.
fix: Run chmod go-w on the file.

file_over_limit.why: Meridian reads its config files, a variable's file, a file of inputs and a worker's bootstrap token's file whole, so it limits their size.
fix: Check that the path names the file you meant, and make the file smaller.

config_yaml_syntax.why: Meridian's config files, groups.yaml and variables.yaml, are YAML.
fix: Fix the YAML at the line the reason names.

config_extra_document.why: Each of Meridian's config files is one YAML document. A second one, after ---, is more likely a mistake than something to ignore.
fix: Remove the --- and what follows it, or move what follows it into the first document.

config_not_mapping.why: groups.yaml maps each group's name to the group, and variables.yaml has org and vars, each a mapping of variables by name.
fix: Write the file as a mapping, as docs/design.md shows.

config_key_unknown.why: Meridian's config files are read strictly, so that a misspelt key is an error rather than a setting that silently does nothing.
fix: Correct the key's spelling, or remove it.

config_key_repeated.why: A key given twice in a mapping in a config file is more likely a mistake than a value to replace: a secret variable written again as a plain one, for example.
fix: Remove one of the two.

config_wrong_type.why: Each key in Meridian's config files takes one type of value.
fix: Give the key a value of the type the message names.

group_name_invalid.why: A group's name is how a job names it, and how an attempt records where it ran.
fix: Rename the group.

group_empty.why: A group is where a job can run: an ordered list of members, each a backend with its settings. A group without members could run nothing.
fix: Give the group a member, or remove it.

member_invalid.why: A member's name has letters, digits, _, - and ., and starts with a letter or a digit. Its backend is local, ssh, kubernetes, slurm or pbs; its isolation names a container runtime, such as podman, or host; its cpu is a number of cores, such as 4 or 0.5, or of thousandths of one, such as 500m; its memory is a number of bytes, or a number with a suffix, such as 8Gi or 512M; and its gpu is a whole number. Its max-walltime, margin and default-timeout are durations greater than 0, written as a workflow's timeout: is: a whole number of seconds, or of minutes, hours or days, such as 3600, 90m, 24h or 1d.
fix: Correct the value as its key needs.

member_repeated.why: A member's name identifies it in its group, and in the record of an attempt placed on it.
fix: Rename one of the members.

variable_name_invalid.why: An expression reads a variable as org.<name> or vars.<name>, so a name can't have a dot or start with a digit.
fix: Rename the variable.

variable_no_value.why: A variable in variables.yaml is its value, or a mapping that says where its value is. One with nothing after its name has neither.
fix: Give the variable a value, or remove it. Write "" for an empty one.

variable_form_invalid.why: A variable in variables.yaml is its value, or a mapping with one of value, the value itself, env, the environment variable it is in, or file, the file it is in, and secret: true for a secret.
fix: Write the variable as text, or as such a mapping.

variable_sources.why: A variable's mapping says where its one value is: in value itself, in an environment variable (env) or in a file (file).
fix: Keep one of value, env and file, and remove the others.

variable_secret_inline.why: A secret's value is kept out of the variables file, so that the file can be read, shared and copied without it.
fix: Move the value into an environment variable, or a file only you can read, and name it with env or file.

variable_env_unset.why: variables.yaml says the variable's value is in an environment variable, which isn't set, or is empty, where Meridian runs. Meridian reads it only when a run reads the variable.
fix: Set the environment variable before running Meridian.
Or change where variables.yaml says the variable's value is.

variable_file_unreadable.why: variables.yaml says the variable's value is in a file, which Meridian reads only when a run reads the variable.
fix: Fix what the reason names, or change where variables.yaml says the variable's value is.

variable_file_home.why: A file's path that starts with ~/ is in your home directory, which Meridian finds with HOME.
fix: Set HOME to your home directory, or write the file's path in full.

cluster_name_invalid.why: A cluster's name is what a compute-clusters input's value names. workspace and user-workspace name this machine, as format 1 names the workspace.
fix: Rename the cluster.

cluster_invalid.why: A cluster needs its host: an alias that ssh resolves, as one in ssh_config, or a host name or an address, without a port, as format 1 gives an existing cluster's ip, which workflows pass to ssh and scp as it is. Its scheduler, if it gives one, is slurm or pbs. Neither can start with - or hold a space.
fix: Correct the value as its key needs.
For a host that needs more, such as a port, a user to log in as, a jump host or an IPv6 address, name an alias that your ssh_config defines.

key_file_invalid.why: The key file holds the 32-byte AES-256 key that wraps the data keys of your runs' secret records. Meridian creates it, and nothing else should change it.
fix: If you have a copy of the key file, put it back.
