Otherwise remove it: Meridian creates another, and the runs whose data keys the old one wrapped can't be resumed.

key_file_missing.why: The key file holds the 32-byte AES-256 key that wraps the data keys of your runs' secret records. Meridian creates it when it first wraps a key, and never makes another in its place to unwrap one: a new key file can't unwrap what the old one wrapped. The key file, or the state directory, has been moved or removed, so the runs whose data keys it wrapped can't read their secret records.
fix: If you have a copy of the key file, or of the state directory, put it back.
Otherwise rerun the runs, whose new data keys a new key file wraps.

key_unwrap_failed.why: Each run's secret record is encrypted under a data key of its own, which the key file's key wraps with AES-256-GCM, bound to the run's ID. A wrapped key that doesn't open was made under another key, moved from another run, or changed.
fix: If the key file was replaced, put back the one that wrapped the run's key.
Otherwise rerun the run, which reads its variables and passwords again.

key_wrapping_unknown.why: A wrapped data key says how it was wrapped, so that a later version of Meridian can wrap keys another way. This one was wrapped by a version this one doesn't know.
fix: Resume the run with the version of Meridian that started it, or a newer one.

git_unavailable.why: Meridian reads the workflows that a step's uses: names from Git repositories by running git, which must be installed and on PATH.
fix: Install git, or put it on PATH.

command_missing.why: The meridian command does one of several things, which its first argument names.
fix: Run meridian help for the commands.

command_unknown.why: The meridian command's first argument names what it does, and this one names nothing it does.
fix: Run meridian help for the commands.

command_not_built.why: Meridian is built in stages, and this command, which docs/design.md describes, comes in a later one.
fix: Use a command that is built, such as meridian validate, or a later release of Meridian.

arguments_invalid.why: Each command takes its own arguments, such as one workflow file.
fix: Run meridian help and the command's name for what it takes.

flag_unknown.why: Each command has its own options.
fix: Run meridian help and the command's name for its options.

flag_needs_value.why: The option takes a value, which follows it, as in -format json, or follows an =, as in -format=json.
fix: Give the option its value.

flag_value_invalid.why: The option takes only some values, which meridian help lists.
fix: Run meridian help and the command's name for the values the option takes.

flag_syntax.why: An option is - or -- and its name, and = and its value if it takes one.
fix: Write the option as -name or -name=value.

input_path_invalid.why: -input sets an input by its path: its name, or its group's name, a dot and its name, as in cluster.size.
fix: Write the path as names joined with dots, without an empty one.

input_path_conflict.why: -input group.name=value sets an input in a group. Here, what the path goes through has a value of its own, from another -input or from the file of inputs.
fix: Give each input one value, and a group's inputs by their paths.

inputs_file_invalid.why: -inputs reads a JSON object of input values by name, in which a key may not appear twice.
fix: Fix the JSON where the reason says.

inputs_file_not_object.why: -inputs reads one JSON object, whose keys are inputs' names and whose values are their values.
fix: Write the values as one JSON object.

inputs_file_extra.why: -inputs reads one JSON object, and something follows it.
fix: Remove what follows the object, or move it into the object.

inputs_number_too_large.why: Meridian reads a number in a file of inputs as a 64-bit number, and this one doesn't fit.
fix: Give the number as text, in quotes, if the input takes text.

interrupted.why: Meridian stopped because it received an interrupt or a request to stop, such as from Ctrl-C.
fix: Run the command again. A second interrupt stops Meridian at once.

unexpected_error.why: An error that Meridian has no more specific problem for stopped the command.
fix: Fix what the reason names, and run the command again.
If it looks like a bug in Meridian, report it with the command you ran.

run_dir_exists.why: Each run has a directory of its own, PW_JOB_DIR, where its steps run, which Meridian makes new once the run is stored, so that no run finds another's files in it, or a link that leads elsewhere. Something is already at the path it would make: a directory named with --run-dir that is there, or one under the system's temporary directory that something else made.
fix: Name a directory that isn't there yet with --run-dir, which Meridian makes.
Or, once you've checked that nothing you need is in it, remove what is at the path, and run the workflow again.

run_dir_not_made.why: Each run has a directory of its own, PW_JOB_DIR, where its steps run, which Meridian makes once the run is stored, or checks it can make before. The operating system refused, for the reason given.
fix: Check that the directory it would be made in is there, and that you can write to it, or name another with --run-dir.

socket_path_too_long.why: Workers on this machine reach the coordinator at a Unix socket in Meridian's state directory, and the system limits how long a socket's path can be. The state directory's path leaves too little room for it.
fix: Set MERIDIAN_STATE_DIR to a directory with a shorter path, on a local disk, which only you can change, and that lasts. It holds the database and the key that wraps your runs' secrets, so move what is in the old one there too.

run_not_found.why: A run is named by its number, which meridian run prints as the run starts. Each state directory has a store of its own, with runs numbered from 1: this one has no run of the number given, as when the number is mistyped, or the run was made with another state directory, as MERIDIAN_STATE_DIR names one.
fix: Run meridian status to see the store's runs, and give the number of one of them.
If the run was made with another state directory, set MERIDIAN_STATE_DIR to it.

job_not_found.why: A job is named by its name in the workflow, or an instance of a matrix job by its key, the name, # and its index, as in build#2. The run has no job of the name given.
fix: Run meridian status with the run's number to see its jobs, and give the name or the key of one of them.

socket_unusable.why: Workers on this machine reach the coordinator at a Unix socket in Meridian's state directory, which one meridian run at a time holds, under a lock beside the database. This one holds the lock, and removes a socket that one that ended left, but the operating system refused to listen there, for the reason given.
fix: Check what is at the path: Meridian replaces only a socket, and leaves anything else for you to remove.
Then run the workflow again.

socket_server_stopped.why: Workers on this machine reach the coordinator at a Unix socket in Meridian's state directory, which meridian run serves until the run ends. Its server stopped while the run went on, without saying why, so the run's workers can no longer report to it.
fix: Check meridian run's other messages for what went wrong, then pick the run up with meridian resume.

coordinator_harden_failed.why: meridian run and meridian resume hold the secret records of the runs they coordinate in their memory: passwords, secret variables and private outputs. Before they open them, they keep your other processes, your runs' steps among them, from reading their memory or attaching to them as a debugger does: on Linux they make themselves not dumpable, on macOS they refuse debuggers (PT_DENY_ATTACH) and set the size of their core file to 0, and on FreeBSD they turn off tracing of themselves (procctl). The operating system refused or failed.
fix: Fix what the reason names, such as a security policy that forbids the call, and run the command again.

coordinator_system_unsupported.why: meridian run and meridian resume hold the secret records of the runs they coordinate in their memory, and keep your other processes, your runs' steps among them, from reading it there. They can on Linux, macOS and FreeBSD. Other systems, such as NetBSD and OpenBSD, give a process no way to keep the user's other processes from tracing it, so Meridian refuses to coordinate a run there, rather than hold its secrets with less protection.
fix: Run the workflow on a machine that runs Linux, macOS or FreeBSD.

source_access_denied.why: The repository asked for credentials git doesn't have, or refused the ones it gave, or its host's key couldn't be checked. A repository that doesn't exist looks the same when the server asks for credentials rather than say so. Meridian never answers a prompt for a password or a passphrase.
fix: Check the reference's owner and repository for a mistake.
Give git credentials it can use without a prompt, such as a credential helper, a token, or an ssh key in your agent, and accept the host's key with ssh beforehand.

source_objects_invalid.why: Meridian has git check every object it fetches, so that a malformed commit or tree, such as one made to exploit a bug in a Git tool, never reaches its copy of the repository.
fix: Find out why the repository has malformed objects, or use another revision.

workflow_calls_itself.why: A step whose uses: names a workflow runs it as a child run, and Meridian pins every workflow the run calls, and those they call, down the tree, as the run is created, as format 1 does. A workflow that is already on its own path of calls would call itself without end, so the run isn't created. The message names the workflows on the path, from the one that calls itself back to it.
fix: Break the cycle: have one of the workflows the message names do the work itself, rather than call the workflow that called it.

workflow_nested_too_deep.why: A step whose uses: names a workflow runs it as a child run, and a child can call workflows too. Meridian pins the whole tree as the run is created, and, as format 1 does, refuses a workflow called more than 4 levels below the run, or as many as whoever runs it allows. The message names the path of calls, from the run's own workflow.
fix: Call fewer workflows deep: have one of the workflows on the path do its callee's work itself.
Or have whoever runs the workflow raise the limit, as Meridian's own limits can be raised.

workflows_too_many.why: Meridian pins every workflow a run calls, and those they call, down the tree, as the run is created. As format 1 does, it allows a tree of at most 100 distinct workflows, and of at most 1,000 calls, each path of calls from the run counted, so that a workflow called from two places counts its own calls twice; or as many as whoever runs it allows. This run's tree has more.
fix: Call fewer workflows, or call the same ones from fewer places.
Or have whoever runs the workflow raise the limit.

workflows_too_large.why: Meridian pins every workflow a run calls, and those they call, down the tree, as the run is created, and keeps their text with the run. As format 1 does, it allows at most 1 MiB of text in all, each distinct workflow counted once, or as much as whoever runs it allows. This run's workflows hold more.
fix: Call fewer, or smaller, workflows.
Or have whoever runs the workflow raise the limit.

child_not_pinned.why: Meridian pins every workflow a run calls, down its tree, as the run is created, and keeps their text with the run, so that each child run runs the text its root was created with. This run was created before Meridian did, so the workflow this step calls isn't among them.
fix: Start the run again: a run created now pins its whole tree.

child_dir_outside.why: A run that a step calls has a directory of its own, subworkflows/<job>/step_<n> under the step's working directory, as in format 1. Meridian makes a root run's directory private, and a child's directory under it is private with it; one elsewhere wouldn't be, and Meridian doesn't make one there yet.
fix: Give the step a working-directory: inside the run's directory, or none.

child_not_created.why: A step whose uses: names a workflow runs it as a run of its own, which the coordinator creates from the step's with: as the step runs, as format 1 does. Creating it failed, as for an input it requires that the with: leaves out, so the step fails, with the run's problems after this one.
fix: Fix the problems that follow, in the step's with: or in the workflow it calls.

owner_unmapped.why: Meridian checks that every directory on the way to its own belongs to you or to root, as OpenSSH checks the way to a user's keys. In a user namespace that doesn't map root, as unshare --user, Apptainer, bubblewrap and some CI sandboxes make, a directory whose owner isn't mapped shows as owned by nobody, so Meridian can't tell who could change it, and refuses it rather than assume.
fix: Run Meridian outside the user namespace, or in one that maps root.

owner_unknown.why: Meridian checks that its own directories and files, and every directory on the way to them, belong to you or to root, as OpenSSH checks the way to a user's keys. This operating system doesn't say who owns a file, so Meridian refuses the path rather than assume that no other user can change it.
fix: Run Meridian on a Unix system, such as Linux or macOS.

directory_replaced.why: A worker keeps its own files in a directory it makes, which only you can use, and holds it open, so that it never uses a path that has come to name something else. Something replaced this one between the worker making it and opening it: a process of yours, such as a job's step, or root's.
fix: Find what removes or replaces directories whose names start with .meridian-worker- in the directory that holds this one, and stop it.

path_links_too_many.why: Meridian follows the symbolic links on the way to its directories, as the kernel does, and stops after as many as the kernel would, which is most likely a link that leads back to itself.
fix: Find the link that leads back to itself, and fix it, or choose another directory.

database_too_new.why: Meridian keeps runs in a database in its state directory, in two schemas: hopper's, which schedules them, and Meridian's own. Each release, as it opens the database, brings each schema up to the version it knows. A release of Meridian newer than this one has opened this database, and this release can't tell what that release changed, so it doesn't open the database, rather than risk the runs in it.
fix: Run the release of Meridian that last opened the database, or a later one.
Or set MERIDIAN_STATE_DIR to another directory, which leaves the runs in this one where they are.

database_too_old.why: Meridian keeps runs in a database in its state directory, whose schema each release that runs workflows, as meridian run and meridian resume do, brings up to the version it knows as it opens the database. A command that only shows runs, as meridian status and meridian logs do, reads the database without changing it, so as not to change a database that an earlier release, still running a workflow, uses; and it can only read a database whose schema is at the version its own release knows. This one is at an earlier version.
fix: Run the command with the release of Meridian that last ran a workflow with this state directory.

Or, once no earlier release of Meridian runs workflows with this state directory, run meridian run or meridian resume with this release, which brings the database up to date, and run the command again.

member_settings_not_json.why: A member's settings are given to its backend's driver as JSON, which has no not-a-number or infinite numbers.
fix: Write the number in the member's settings as a finite one, or as text in quotes.

worker_environment_missing.why: A backend starts meridian worker with the coordinator's address in MERIDIAN_COORDINATOR, and the attempt's bootstrap token in MERIDIAN_BOOTSTRAP_TOKEN, or in a file MERIDIAN_BOOTSTRAP_TOKEN_FILE names, never on its command line. Without them, the worker can't claim an attempt.
fix: Let a backend start meridian worker: people don't run it.

worker_environment_invalid.why: MERIDIAN_COORDINATOR_KEY_SHA256 must be sha256: and 64 hex digits when the coordinator is reached over TLS, and unset when it is a Unix socket; and only one of MERIDIAN_BOOTSTRAP_TOKEN and MERIDIAN_BOOTSTRAP_TOKEN_FILE may be set.
fix: Let a backend start meridian worker, which sets them as it should.

coordinator_peer_refused.why: A worker sends its bootstrap token, and then the attempt's credential, only to a coordinator of its own user's, or root's. It asks the operating system who serves the socket, and another user does: one who could have put a socket at that path to take the token.
fix: Start the worker with the socket of a coordinator you run, in a directory only you can change.

coordinator_peer_unknown.why: A worker sends its bootstrap token, and then the attempt's credential, only to a coordinator of its own user's, or root's, and asks the operating system who serves the socket before it sends anything. The operating system didn't say.
fix: Fix what the reason names, and let the backend start the worker again.

coordinator_key_mismatch.why: A worker reaches a coordinator over TLS by its key: the backend gives it the SHA-256 hash of the coordinator's public key, and the worker talks only to a server that holds that key, whatever its certificate says. This server holds another.
fix: Check that MERIDIAN_COORDINATOR names the coordinator, or its relay, and that the coordinator's replicas share one key.

coordinator_answer_invalid.why: A worker reads the coordinator's answers strictly, as the worker API's version defines them, and the coordinator refuses a request with a problem that has a code. This answer was neither, or was larger than a refusal can be, so the worker stopped, rather than guess what the coordinator meant. A worker and a coordinator of different releases of Meridian, or a server that isn't the coordinator, answer so.
fix: Start workers of the same release of Meridian as the coordinator, and check that the worker reaches the coordinator, not another server.

coordinator_lost_data.why: A worker keeps what it reports only until the coordinator says it has stored it. This coordinator then asked for it again, from earlier, as one that lost what it had stored would, such as one whose database was restored from a backup. The worker stops the job, rather than leave a hole in what the run records.
fix: Find out why the coordinator lost what it had stored. The job runs again if its retry: lists worker-lost.

coordinator_stored_unsent.why: A worker numbers the events it reports, and the coordinator answers with the number of the last it has stored. One past those the worker sent means that the coordinator holds events this worker never sent, as one that mixed two attempts up would, so the worker stops, rather than go on reporting to it.
fix: Report the bug, with the coordinator's and the worker's logs.

bootstrap_token_refused.why: A bootstrap token claims one attempt, once: the coordinator refuses it once the attempt is claimed, by this worker with another credential, or by another, or once its placement is withdrawn. The worker exits, and runs nothing.
fix: Nothing to fix if the attempt was cancelled; otherwise, let the backend start a worker with the attempt's own token.

bootstrap_token_in_environment.why: A bootstrap token claims its attempt once, for whoever presents it first. On macOS, any process of a user can read the arguments and environment of any other of theirs, as ps -E does, whatever the worker does to protect itself, so another process, such as a step of another job, could read the token there and claim the attempt. The worker takes a token from a file instead, which it removes as soon as it has read it.
fix: Give the token in a file only you can read, whose path MERIDIAN_BOOTSTRAP_TOKEN_FILE names, rather than in MERIDIAN_BOOTSTRAP_TOKEN.

run_plan_too_new.why: A run's plan is versioned, and a worker runs only a plan of a version it reads, so that it never runs a job without a part of it it doesn't understand. The coordinator refused the claim before it sent anything of the run. No step ran, so the attempt is placed again.
fix: Start workers of the same release of Meridian as the coordinator.

attempt_superseded.why: Every report a worker sends carries the attempt's credential, and the coordinator stores it only while the attempt holds the job. Another attempt of the job superseded this one, or the attempt ended without this worker, as when its lease lapsed. The worker stops the job's steps, without their cleanup: commands, which another attempt could be relying on, and exits.
fix: Nothing to fix: the coordinator decides how the attempt ended, and whether the job runs again.

attempt_lease_lapsed.why: A job whose retry: lists worker-lost can run again while this attempt may still run, cut off, so its worker stops it before its lease lapses: once it hasn't renewed the lease for six tenths of it, it stops every process the attempt started, and by nine tenths has killed them. The coordinator could not be reached for that long. Its new attempt resumes the job, as its retry: asks.
fix: Check the connection between the host the job ran on and the coordinator, and that the job's lease is long enough to ride out the outages you expect.

worker_harden_failed.why: A worker holds the attempt's credential in its memory, so before it claims the attempt it keeps your other processes, a job's steps among them, from reading its memory or attaching to it as a debugger does: on Linux it makes itself not dumpable, on macOS it refuses debuggers (PT_DENY_ATTACH) and sets the size of its core file to 0, and on FreeBSD it turns off tracing of itself (procctl). The operating system refused or failed.
fix: Fix what the reason names, such as a security policy that forbids the call, and let the backend start the worker again.

worker_system_unsupported.why: A worker holds the attempt's credential in its memory, and keeps your other processes, a job's steps among them, from reading it there or tracing what it sends. It can on Linux, macOS and FreeBSD. Other systems, such as NetBSD and OpenBSD, give a process no way to keep the user's other processes from tracing it, so the worker refuses to run there, rather than run a job with less protection.
fix: Run the job on a member whose hosts run Linux, macOS or FreeBSD.

source_server_unknown.why: A step's with: $host names the GitLab server that holds the workflow its uses: names. Git reaches a server with the user's own configuration and credentials, so Meridian reaches only gitlab.com and the servers the user registered, rather than any a workflow names: locally, those that sources.yaml, in the config directory, lists under gitlab-servers.
fix: If you trust the server, add it to gitlab-servers in sources.yaml, by its name, as git.example.com.
Otherwise, use a workflow from a server that is registered.

compute_target_unknown.why: A format 1 job's runs-on: can give a compute target, as a compute-target input's value does: a mode, login, worker or environment, and a target, which only a platform knows. Where the workflow runs, the Groups interface has no such compute target: locally there are none.
fix: Run the workflow on the platform that has the compute target, or run the job in an execution group instead (runs-on: execution-group:).

gitlab_server_invalid.why: sources.yaml's gitlab-servers lists the GitLab servers, besides gitlab.com, that a workflow's with: $host can name. Each is a server's DNS name, as a $host names it, with no port, as ACTIVATE reads a $host: Meridian adds the scheme and reaches the server at HTTPS's port, and a server has no user or path.
fix: Write the server as git.example.com.

For a server at another port, register its name, and have Git reach it at its port with Git's url.<base>.insteadOf setting, as in: git config --global url.https://git.example.com:8443/.insteadOf https://git.example.com/

source_with_invalid.why: A step's with: $host names the GitLab server that holds the workflow its uses: names, by its DNS name, with no port, as ACTIVATE reads it; and $yaml names the workflow's file in the repository by its path from the repository's root. A path that starts with a slash is from the root, as ACTIVATE fetches the file: every slash before it goes on GitHub, and one on GitLab. No name in the path can be empty, as ./ or a doubled slash makes one, nor . or .., nor hold a control character, so that the path names a file among the repository's own.
fix: Write the server as git.example.com, and the file as flows/workflow.yaml.

input_read_as_submitted.why: Format 1 reads each input's value as it was submitted, as ACTIVATE does, and converts none: text submitted for a number or a boolean input stays text, and a number or a boolean submitted for a text input stays a number or a boolean. ACTIVATE's run form sends a number field's value as a JSON number and a checkbox's as a JSON boolean, so a value like this comes from a caller that wrote it as another JSON type. What reads the input reads the value as it is: the text "false" isn't empty, so an if: reads it as true.
fix: Submit the value as its input's JSON type: 5, not "5", for a number, and false, not "false", for a boolean.
meridian validate -input converts a value by its input's type, as ACTIVATE's pw workflows run --input does.

flattened_group_value.why: A group with flatten: true has its inputs' values beside its own, under their own names, as ACTIVATE runs it, so a value at the group's key, given for the run or written in a list's default row, isn't its inputs'. It is kept as it is, as ACTIVATE keeps it, as a secret if the group has a password among its inputs, and what reads inputs.<group> reads it; if the group is ignored, it is dropped with the group's inputs.
fix: Give the group's inputs their values by their own names, beside the group's, or remove the value.

flattened_name_taken.why: A group with flatten: true has its inputs' values beside its own, under their own names, so each of them needs a name that no other input whose value is there has, the group's own among them. ACTIVATE fills such a value from both definitions, in the order the file writes them, which the workflow's meaning shouldn't depend on, so Meridian refuses it, where ACTIVATE runs it.
fix: Rename one of the inputs, or remove the group's flatten: true.

input_flag_unsplit.why: -input sets one input, as path=value. Without an =, there is no path, and the problem doesn't repeat what was given, which can be a password.
fix: Write it as path=value, as -input nodes=8.

input_flag_wrong_type.why: -input converts its value by the type of the input it sets, as ACTIVATE's pw workflows run --input does: a boolean input takes true or false, exactly; a number input a JSON number, so 007, 0x10, +1, .5 and 1. aren't one, nor is a number too large for 64 bits; and a header takes no value. The problem doesn't repeat the value, which can be a password.
fix: Give the input a value of its type, as -input debug=false or -input nodes=8.

input_flag_not_json.why: A list, a multi-dropdown, a repeated wizard step, a group, a wizard step, a compute target, and a compute-clusters, compute-resources or bucket input with multi: true take a structure, which -input reads as JSON, as ACTIVATE's pw workflows run --input does. The problem says where the JSON goes wrong, by byte, and doesn't repeat the value, which can hold a password.
fix: Write the value as JSON, quoted for the shell, as -input 'files=["a.txt"]'.

input_flag_wrong_shape.why: -input reads a structure's value as JSON, which must be the shape its input takes, as ACTIVATE's pw workflows run --input reads it: an array for a list, a multi-dropdown, a repeated wizard step and a multi input, and an object for a group, a wizard step and a compute target.
fix: Write the value as the JSON its input takes: an array, in square brackets, or an object, in braces.

input_flag_path_not_settable.why: A path is an input's name, or a group's name and its input's, as group.name, as ACTIVATE's pw workflows run --input reads one. A wizard step that flattens, as one does unless $meta.wizard.flatten is false, and a group with flatten: true put their inputs beside them, so those inputs are set by their own names; a list, or a repeated wizard step, is set whole, as JSON; and an input that holds no inputs has none to set.
fix: Name the input by its own name, or set the list whole, as JSON.

fenced.why: The coordinator checks every write against the attempt's fencing number, so that an attempt another of its job has superseded, as when its lease lapsed and the job ran again, can't change what the run records. A report from an attempt that has completed, other than one repeated as it was, is refused the same way. The worker stops its job's steps, as a cancellation does, and exits.
fix: Nothing to fix: the coordinator decides how the attempt ended, and whether the job runs again.

out_of_order.why: A worker numbers its events and sends a log's bytes from an offset, so that a report repeated after a dropped connection is stored once, and in order. This one skipped some, started past the end of the log or after it had ended, or ended the attempt before the coordinator had every event it counts. The worker sends again from where the coordinator expects.
fix: Nothing to fix: the worker sends again from where the coordinator expects.

plan_too_new.why: A run's plan is versioned, and a worker says the newest plan version it reads as it claims an attempt. The coordinator refuses one that doesn't read the run's, before it sends anything of the run, so that no worker runs a job with a part it doesn't understand. The worker exits, and the attempt, which failed before its first step, is placed again.
fix: Start workers of the same release of Meridian as the coordinator.

worker_api_too_old.why: The worker API has a version of its own, apart from the plan's, which each addition to it raises, and a worker says the newest version it speaks as it claims an attempt. The coordinator refuses a worker whose version is older than the oldest that has everything the attempt's job uses, before it sends anything of the run, rather than run the job without that part. The worker exits, and the attempt, which failed before its first step, is placed again.
fix: Start workers of the same release of Meridian as the coordinator, or of a later one.

worker_digest_mismatch.why: A backend records the SHA-256 digest of the meridian binary it starts for an attempt, and a worker says its own as it claims the attempt. The coordinator refuses a claim whose digest isn't the one recorded, before it sends anything of the run: the binary was replaced between the placement and the claim, or another program claimed with the attempt's bootstrap token. The attempt fails before its first step, and is placed again.
fix: If Meridian was upgraded while the job was being placed, nothing needs doing: the job is placed again, with the new binary.
Otherwise find out what replaced the binary, or what else read the attempt's bootstrap token.

fips_not_enforced.why: Meridian is built with Go's validated FIPS 140-3 cryptographic module, and runs only with GODEBUG's fips140=only, which makes the use of an algorithm the module doesn't approve an error. The binary makes fips140=only its default, but the GODEBUG environment variable overrides a default, and a worker can be started by hand or over SSH with any environment. So every meridian command, the worker above all, refuses to run without it, rather than run with weaker cryptography.
fix: Remove fips140 from GODEBUG, or set it to fips140=only, and run the command again.
In a program that runs Meridian's worker itself (worker.Run), make fips140=only its default: add godebug fips140=only to its go.mod, or //go:debug fips140=only to its main package.

fips_module_not_validated.why: Go's FIPS 140-3 module is validated in the frozen versions that GOFIPS140 names as it builds a program, such as certified. A build without GOFIPS140 compiles the module from Go's source, as the version latest, which isn't the validated module, whatever mode it runs in. Meridian refuses to run with it, rather than run with cryptography that isn't validated.
fix: Build meridian with GOFIPS140=certified: with make build in its repository, with GOFIPS140=certified go install github.com/parallelworks/meridian/cmd/meridian@ and the version, or once for every build with go env -w GOFIPS140=certified.

isolation_not_built.why: A member names how it isolates the jobs placed on it: a container runtime, such as podman, docker or apptainer, or host, which runs a job's steps on the host, as you. A member that names none isolates them in a rootless container. The local backend runs jobs on the host only, today, and Meridian never runs a job with weaker isolation than its member names, so placement leaves the member out, and places the job on another member of its group if there is one.
fix: Name host isolation for the member in groups.yaml, if running its jobs' steps on the host, as you, is what you want.

resources_exceed_member.why: A member offers the resources it declares in groups.yaml or, for one of the local backend that declares none, the host's CPUs and memory, and no GPU unless it declares some. A job whose resources: asks for more than that can never run there, so placement leaves the member out, and places the job on another member of its group if one offers enough.
fix: Ask for less in the job's resources:, declare what the member offers in groups.yaml, or run the job in a group with a member that offers enough.

backend_not_built.why: A member names the backend that starts workers on it: local, ssh, kubernetes, slurm or pbs. This release of Meridian has only the local backend, so placement leaves a member of another backend out, and places the job on another member of its group if there is one.
fix: Run the job in a group with a member of the local backend, until a release has the member's backend.

worker_binary_unsafe.why: The local backend starts each worker from the meridian binary that places it, and the worker holds the attempt's credential once it runs. So the binary must be a regular file of yours or root's that no other user can change, nor any directory on the way to it: otherwise another user could replace it with a program that reads what the worker is given. The code is the problem with it, and its page says why.
fix: Fix what the code's page says, for the binary the message names, or install meridian where only you or root can change it, such as /usr/local/bin.

ssh_host_key_unknown.why: Meridian checks every host's key against your known_hosts files, those your SSH configuration names (UserKnownHostsFile and GlobalKnownHostsFile), as ssh does, by the host's HostKeyAlias, or else its name and port, and refuses a key it doesn't find there. It never adds one itself, whatever StrictHostKeyChecking says: a key taken on trust the first time is how a first connection is taken over. A key of a type known_hosts has none of for the host is unknown too.
fix: Check the key's fingerprint with the host's administrator, or on the host, with ssh-keygen -lf on its key, then add the key to known_hosts, as ssh <host> offers to, answering yes only if the fingerprint matches.
If known_hosts has the host's key under another name, set HostKeyAlias for the host in your SSH configuration.

ssh_host_key_changed.why: The key the host presented differs from the key of the same type that your known_hosts has for it. Either the host's key was replaced, as when it was reinstalled, or another machine is answering for it, which is what the check is there to catch.
fix: Ask the host's administrator whether its key changed, and check the new key's fingerprint.
If it did, remove the old key with ssh-keygen -R <host>, and add the new one, as for a host you connect to the first time.

ssh_host_key_revoked.why: Your known_hosts marks the key @revoked, or the file your SSH configuration's RevokedHostKeys names lists it, or, for a host certificate, its key or its authority's: whoever manages them has said not to trust it, for any host.
fix: Ask the host's administrator for its current key, and add it to known_hosts once you have checked its fingerprint.

ssh_algorithms_unapproved.why: Meridian runs in FIPS 140-3 mode, which lets it use only the algorithms the standard approves. For SSH, those it can run are key exchange with ECDH on the NIST curves P-256, P-384 and P-521, the ciphers aes128-ctr, aes192-ctr and aes256-ctr, the MACs hmac-sha2-256 and hmac-sha2-512, and host keys of ECDSA, Ed25519, or RSA signing with SHA-2. AES-GCM and the hybrid ML-KEM key exchange are approved too, but the SSH library can't run them in this mode yet. A host that offers none of one of these, as one that offers only curve25519 or chacha20-poly1305 does, can't be used.
fix: Ask the host's administrator to add the algorithms Meridian needs to the server's configuration: KexAlgorithms, Ciphers, MACs and HostKeyAlgorithms in sshd_config.

ssh_auth_failed.why: Meridian logs in with the keys of your SSH agent, then the key files your SSH configuration names for the host (IdentityFile), then your other key pairs in ~/.ssh, each a private key beside its .pub, unless IdentitiesOnly is set. It never asks for a passphrase, so a key file that needs one is offered only if your agent holds its key, and it never logs in with a password. It doesn't offer DSA keys, or RSA keys of fewer than 2048 bits, which FIPS 140-3 doesn't let it sign with. The host accepted none of the keys it offered, or it had none to offer.
fix: Check that the key you log in to the host with is in your agent (ssh-add -l), or is a key file without a passphrase that your configuration names for the host.
Check that the user is the one you mean, remoteUser, or else User in your configuration, or else your own, and that the host has the key's public half in that user's authorized_keys.
Run ssh -v <host> to see which keys ssh offers, and which the host accepts.

ssh_config_unreadable.why: Meridian reads your SSH configuration for each host as ssh does, by running ssh -G, and connects as it says: its HostName, Port, User, IdentityFile, ProxyJump, ProxyCommand, known_hosts files and HostKeyAlias. ssh couldn't read the configuration, a file it names, such as a known_hosts file, couldn't be read, or what it says can't be used, as a ProxyCommand with a token Meridian doesn't know, or ProxyJumps that lead back to themselves.
fix: Run ssh -G <host> to see what ssh says, and fix your configuration, or the file, where it points.

ssh_config_not_read.why: Meridian reads your SSH configuration through ssh, by running ssh -G. Without an ssh client on PATH, and with no configuration for one to read, neither yours (~/.ssh/config) nor the system's (/etc/ssh/ssh_config), it uses OpenSSH's defaults: the host as it is named, port 22, your own user name, the key files in ~/.ssh with OpenSSH's default names, your agent, and the known_hosts files in ~/.ssh and /etc/ssh.
fix: Install OpenSSH's client, or put it on PATH, if your configuration says how to reach the host.

ssh_config_output_unexpected.why: Meridian reads your SSH configuration for each host by running ssh -G, which prints a keyword and its value on each line, and takes that only as OpenSSH's ssh prints it: each keyword it reads on one line, but IdentityFile, which ssh prints for each key file, and the host and the port as Meridian asked for them. Output otherwise could hold lines that aren't your configuration's: an ssh before OpenSSH 10.1 prints a user it is given as it is, so a newline in one starts a line of its own, which could pass for a ProxyCommand. Meridian gives ssh only a user that holds no control character, so the ssh client on PATH, or something that wraps it, printed this itself.
fix: Run ssh -G <host> and look at the keyword the message names: OpenSSH's own client prints it once.
Put OpenSSH's own client first on PATH, if the ssh there wraps it.

ssh_revoked_host_keys_unreadable.why: Your SSH configuration's RevokedHostKeys names a file of host keys that are revoked: a list of public keys, one to a line, or a KRL, OpenSSH's binary list, which Meridian checks a key against with ssh-keygen -Q. Where the file isn't there, can't be read, or is a KRL that ssh-keygen can't check, as where there is no ssh-keygen beside ssh, Meridian can't tell whether it revokes the host's key, or its certificate's authority, so it trusts no key of the host's, as OpenSSH trusts none.
fix: Check that the file is there, and that you can read it, or remove RevokedHostKeys from your configuration if it shouldn't apply to the host.
For a KRL, install OpenSSH's ssh-keygen beside ssh.

ssh_known_hosts_command.why: KnownHostsCommand runs a command that prints more known_hosts lines for a host, which can revoke a key as well as name one. Meridian checks host keys itself, against the known_hosts files your configuration names, and doesn't run the command, so it can't know what the command would revoke; it doesn't connect, rather than check the host's key against part of what you've said of it.
fix: Put the host's keys, and any that are revoked, in a known_hosts file your configuration names, and set KnownHostsCommand none for the host, in a Host or Match block.

ssh_client_missing.why: Meridian reads your SSH configuration through ssh, by running ssh -G, which applies Match, Include and the rest as ssh would. Without an ssh client on PATH, Meridian can use OpenSSH's defaults only where there is no configuration to read, neither yours (~/.ssh/config) nor the system's (/etc/ssh/ssh_config): what one says, as how to reach the host, or a host key it revokes, can't be ignored.
fix: Install OpenSSH's client, or put it on PATH.

ssh_command_unsafe.why: Meridian runs ssh to read your SSH configuration, ssh-keygen to match hashed known_hosts lines and to check a KRL, and your shell, SHELL, or else /bin/sh, to run a ProxyCommand, with your agent, your keys and your connections to hosts at hand. So before it runs one, it checks that it is a regular file of yours or root's that no other user can change, nor any directory on the way to it, as the local backend checks a command it runs. A directory another user can change can come first on PATH, as a shared bin/ that a cluster's startup files add, and a command they put there would run as you. The code in the message is the problem with the command, whose own page says more.
fix: Take away the write permission other users have on the command, or on the directory on the way to it, as the code's page says, or put a directory only you and root can change first on PATH.
Set SHELL to a shell that is safe to run, if the command is your shell.

ssh_target_unsafe.why: A format 1 ssh:'s remoteHost, remoteUser, jumpNodeHost and jumpNodeUser often come from a workflow's inputs. Meridian gives ssh the host and the user, to read your configuration for, and both can reach a ProxyCommand there, which a shell runs with them in it. So, as OpenSSH 10.1 and later checks its own command line, Meridian refuses a host that starts with -, or holds white space, a control character, or any of ' ` " $ \ ; & < > | ( ) { }, and a user that starts with -, holds a control character, as a newline, or any of ' ` " ; & < > | ( ) { }, has - after white space, or ends with \, whatever ssh is installed. The message shows the value with its control characters escaped, as \n.
fix: Give the input a host's name or address, or a user's name, as the workflow expects.

ssh_host_form_unsupported.why: A format 1 ssh:'s remoteHost and jumpNodeHost each name one host: its name or address, as your SSH configuration may know it, or a host and its port, host:port. Its user is remoteUser or jumpNodeUser. ssh's own command line takes more: a user in the host, user@host, a URL, ssh://user@host:port, and for -J a list of hosts, a,b. Meridian reads your configuration for a host with ssh -G, which would take the user out of the host and print another host than Meridian asked for, and Meridian would dial a list as one host's name. So it refuses a host that holds @, :// or a comma, before it connects anywhere.
fix: Give remoteHost or jumpNodeHost the host alone, or host:port, and its user in remoteUser or jumpNodeUser.
To connect through more than one jump host, name the last in jumpNodeHost, and the others in a ProxyJump for it in your SSH configuration.

ssh_known_hosts_unmatched.why: A hashed known_hosts line, which HashKnownHosts writes, keeps its host as an HMAC-SHA1 of it, which FIPS 140-3 doesn't let Meridian compute, so Meridian asks ssh-keygen -F which hashed lines are the host's. Without it, Meridian can't tell whether a hashed line revokes the host's key, so it doesn't check the key against the rest of the file: that could accept a key known_hosts revokes.
fix: Install OpenSSH's ssh-keygen, or put it on PATH beside ssh.
Or keep the host's keys, and any @revoked lines, in a known_hosts file without hashed lines, which your configuration names.

ssh_host_certificate_invalid.why: An authority that known_hosts names for the host (@cert-authority) signed the certificate, but it isn't valid for this connection: it has expired, isn't valid yet, isn't for this host's name, or isn't a host certificate. Meridian doesn't fall back to the certificate's key then, as OpenSSH falls back only when no authority it knows signed the certificate.
fix: Ask the host's administrator to renew the host's certificate, or to sign it for the name you connect to.

ssh_proxy_command_token.why: Meridian runs your configuration's ProxyCommand through sh -c, as ssh does, with the tokens %h, %p, %r, %n, %u, %d and %% expanded. It doesn't run one that holds another, which it would pass to the command as it is.
fix: Write the ProxyCommand with the tokens Meridian expands, or with what the token stands for.

ssh_proxy_jump_too_deep.why: Meridian follows your configuration's ProxyJump through each host it names, and each of those hosts' own ProxyJump, to at most this many hosts deep. Deeper, the ProxyJumps lead back to themselves, as a host whose ProxyJump names a host whose ProxyJump names it does.
fix: Run ssh -G <host> for each host the ProxyJumps name, and break the loop in your configuration.

ssh_proxy_jump_invalid.why: Each of a ProxyJump's hosts is [user@]host[:port], or ssh://[user@]host[:port]. This one names no host, or its host or user holds what Meridian doesn't give ssh, as it doesn't a workflow's (ssh_target_unsafe): a control character, or a character a shell reads as more than a name. The message shows the hop with its control characters escaped.
fix: Fix the ProxyJump in your configuration, as ssh -G <host> shows it.

ssh_host_unsupported.why: Meridian runs a job on a host with its worker, the meridian binary, which runs on Linux, macOS and FreeBSD, on amd64, arm64, 386 and arm. The host's uname says another system, which the worker can't protect its memory on, or isn't built for.
fix: Run the job on a host of one of those systems, through its ssh:, or a group that names one.

ssh_worker_binary_missing.why: A host of the coordinator's own system runs the coordinator's binary, copied there. A host of another system, or another architecture, needs this release's binary built for it, which Meridian never fetches by itself: it runs one only once you have put it where it looks, checked against the release's checksums.
fix: Download this release's meridian binary for the host's system, check it against the release's published checksums, and put it at the path, in directories only you can open.
Or run the job on a host of the coordinator's own system.

ssh_worker_binary_unverified.why: Meridian copies the worker's binary to a host into a file of its own in a directory only you can open, and keeps it only once its SHA-256 digest there is the binary's, computed with the host's sha256sum, shasum, sha256 or openssl. The copy isn't the binary, as when it was cut short or changed on the way, and was removed; or the host has none of those tools, so the copy can't be checked, and isn't run.
fix: If the host has no tool to compute a SHA-256 digest, install one of them there: coreutils' sha256sum, Perl's shasum, FreeBSD's sha256 or OpenSSL.
If the digest differed, run the job again: Meridian copies the binary again. If it differs again, something on the host or on the way changes the file.

ssh_host_missing.why: A member of the ssh backend, as a format 1 job's ssh: makes, runs jobs on the host its remoteHost names. This member's remoteHost is empty or null, so there is no host to run the job on.
fix: Give the job's ssh: a remoteHost, a host's name or address, or, where it reads one from an input, give the input one.

ssh_unreachable.why: Before a job is placed on a host, Meridian connects to it, and tries four times, as format 1 does, each try bounded by the host's ConnectTimeout, or 30 seconds. Format 1 waits 2, 4 and 8 seconds between its tries; Meridian waits about 1, 2 and 4, as it does before it dials any host again that it failed to reach. The host didn't answer, or the connection failed each time: its name doesn't resolve, nothing listens on its port, a jump host or a ProxyCommand on the way failed, or a network or a VPN between is down. The job isn't placed there, and fails, as format 1's step does.
fix: Run ssh -v <host> from the same machine, as the same user, to see where the connection fails.
Check the host's name, its port and its jump host, in the workflow's ssh: and in your SSH configuration, and that the network to it is up.

ssh_host_helper_failed.why: Meridian runs a job on a host through meridian host, Meridian's own binary, which it copies there, and which answers it in a protocol of its own over SSH. This time meridian host stopped before it answered, and said why on its standard error, as meridian says a problem before it runs a command: as one does whose binary isn't built with the FIPS 140-3 module, or doesn't run in FIPS 140-only mode, which every meridian command requires.
fix: Read the reason: it is meridian's own message, with its code, whose page says more.
Run the coordinator from a release of Meridian, built with the FIPS 140-3 module, so that the binary it copies to the host is one too.

ssh_forwarding_refused.why: A worker on a host reaches the coordinator through a Unix socket on the host, which sshd listens on for the coordinator, and forwards over its SSH connection (streamlocal-forward@openssh.com, as ssh -R does with a socket's path). Meridian opens no port, on either side. sshd refused: it doesn't forward Unix sockets, as with AllowStreamLocalForwarding no or DisableForwarding yes in sshd_config, or it couldn't listen at the path.
fix: Ask the host's administrators to allow forwarding Unix sockets: AllowStreamLocalForwarding yes, or all, in sshd_config.
Check that ssh -R <path>:/dev/null <host> true can forward a socket there, from the same machine and user.

ssh_host_release_mismatch.why: Meridian copies its own binary to a host, and drives meridian host there, which must be of the coordinator's release, as the binary it copied is. meridian host said another release: the binary in the host's cache of binaries isn't the one Meridian copied, or a binary fetched for the host's system is of another release.
fix: Remove the host's cache of binaries, the bin/ of meridian's cache directory there, so that Meridian copies its binary again.
If the host is of another system than the coordinator's, fetch this release's binary for it again.

ssh_placement_elsewhere.why: A host's name can lead to more than one machine, as a cluster's login nodes behind one name do, each of which keeps its own workers. Meridian placed the worker on one of them, and connecting again reached another, which knows nothing of it. Meridian takes such a worker to run for a while, as it does over a connection that is down, and then to be lost, with this problem: the node it is on may be down, gone, or out of the name's rotation.
fix: Check whether the node the job ran on is up, and in the name's rotation.
Where a cluster's login nodes share a name, and its jobs must reach the same one, name a node itself, in the workflow's ssh: or in the clusters file.

worker_token_not_taken.why: Where the process that places a worker ends once it has, as meridian host does on another host, it waits until the worker has taken its bootstrap token, which it hands over on a socket only the worker inherits. This worker didn't: it ended first, as one that systemd-run couldn't start does, where your service manager can't be reached or a scope of the same name is still there, or it didn't ask for its token within a minute. A worker without its token can't run the job, so Meridian stopped it, and placed nothing.
fix: Read the file the message names, on the host, for what the worker, or what started it, wrote.
If systemd-run says it can't reach your service manager, check that systemctl --user status works on the host, in a session over SSH such as the coordinator opens.

ssh_worker_would_be_killed.why: On a host, each worker is started from a session the coordinator opens there, and it must outlive that session, to run the job's steps and report them after the session has ended. This host's logind ends every process of a session as the session ends (KillUserProcesses=yes), and you don't linger there, so your service manager, in which Meridian would start the worker instead, stops after your last session too. A worker started on the host would end as soon as the coordinator's session did, so Meridian doesn't start one.
fix: Run loginctl enable-linger on the host, as yourself, which keeps your service manager running after your last session: Meridian then starts workers in it.
Or ask the host's administrators to set KillUserProcesses=no in logind.conf, as most systems have it.

ssh_host_dir_unusable.why: On a host, Meridian keeps what it keeps in directories of your own: the local backend's state, the workers' binaries and runs' directories, in your state and cache directories; and the sockets the coordinator listens on for the host's workers, in your runtime directory (XDG_RUNTIME_DIR), or else in a directory of a random name that Meridian makes in /tmp, so that no other user can make it first. Each must be one that only you can use, on a way no other user can change, since what is in it, or reaches a worker through it, is yours alone. Meridian makes the one that isn't there, and checks each: this one failed at the path the message names, the directory itself or one on the way to it, for the reason given, a problem's code, whose page says why, or the system's error.
fix: Fix what the reason says, for the path the message names, on the host: chmod 700, for a directory of yours that other users can use.
If what holds it can't be yours alone, set XDG_STATE_HOME or XDG_CACHE_HOME on the host to a directory of your own, as for Meridian's state and cache directories anywhere.

ssh_host_command_unsafe.why: On a host, meridian host runs commands of the system's that it finds on the PATH: loginctl, to ask logind whether a session's processes end with it; systemd-run, which starts a worker in a scope of your service manager, and so gets what the worker is given, the socket its bootstrap token comes on among it; and, on macOS, ioreg, for the host's ID. So each must be a regular file of yours or root's that no other user can change, nor any directory on the way to it: otherwise another user could put a program of theirs first on your PATH, in a directory they can change, and take what it is given. The code is the problem with it, and its page says why.
fix: Take the directory that other users can change out of your PATH on the host, where your shell's startup files set it, or put it after the system's directories, such as /usr/bin.
Or fix what the code's page says, for the command the message names.

ssh_host_id_unknown.why: On a host, Meridian keeps the local backend's state in a directory of the host's own, named by the host's machine ID and its name, so that hosts that share a home, as a cluster's nodes do, don't take each other's workers for their own. On Linux the ID is systemd's, in /etc/machine-id, or else D-Bus's, in /var/lib/dbus/machine-id; on macOS, the hardware's UUID; on FreeBSD, the kernel's kern.hostuuid. This host has none that Meridian can read, as where the file isn't there, is empty or says uninitialized, or holds what a directory's name can't; or the host says no name.
fix: Ask the host's administrators to give it a machine ID: on Linux, with systemd-machine-id-setup, or dbus-uuidgen --ensure where there is no systemd.
If hostname says no name on the host, ask them to give it one.

ssh_loginctl_missing.why: On a host, each worker must outlive the session the coordinator opens there to start it. Where logind runs, it ends a session's processes as the session ends if it is set to (KillUserProcesses=yes), so Meridian asks it, with loginctl, which it finds on the PATH. logind runs on this host, but the PATH there finds no loginctl, so Meridian can't tell whether a worker would end with its session, and starts none, rather than one that might.
fix: Put the directory that holds loginctl, usually /usr/bin, on your PATH on the host, where your shell's startup files set it.
Or ask the host's administrators to install it, with systemd.

ssh_systemd_too_old.why: On a host whose logind ends a session's processes as the session ends, and where you linger, Meridian starts each worker in a scope of your service manager, with systemd-run --user --scope --collect, so that it outlives the session that starts it. --collect, with which a scope that failed goes once it has ended, rather than stay loaded until someone resets it, came with systemd 236. This host's systemd-run is older, so Meridian starts no worker there, rather than one whose scope a failure would leave behind.
fix: Ask the host's administrators to set KillUserProcesses=no in logind.conf, as most systems have it: Meridian then starts workers in a session of their own, without systemd-run.
Or run the job on a host with systemd 236 or later.
